text: Week 11 — Spatial point processes

title: Week 11 tutorial: Spatial point processes
text:
Overview
In weeks 7 to 10 the locations were fixed and you modelled a value measured at them. Here the locations are the data: what you model is where the points fall and how many there are.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

load and visualise a spatial point pattern;
explore its first-order (intensity) and second-order (interaction) properties;
fit homogeneous and inhomogeneous Poisson process models; and
assess goodness of fit, and say what a simulation envelope is testing.


The data
The ants data record the nests of two ant species, Messor wasmanni and Cataglyphis bicolor, at a site in northern Greece. There are 97 nests in all — 68 Messor and 29 Cataglyphis — within an irregular polygonal sampling window. The species label is carried as a mark on each point, so this is a marked point pattern; the questions below mostly treat the nests as a single unmarked pattern.
The data come with spatstat.data rather than with the course package, so you load them with data(ants) after attaching that package.

title: Week 11 tutorial: Spatial point processes
section: Q1: exploring and modelling a point pattern
text:
Q1: exploring and modelling a point pattern

Load and plot the ant nest point pattern, and summarise it.











`data(ants)` from `spatstat.data`. `plot()` shows the pattern and `summary()`
gives the window, the number of points and the average intensity.
Look at the pattern first and form an opinion before you compute anything: does
it look clustered, regular, or neither?



What this shows

The ant nest pattern, and the summary gives the window, the number of points and the average intensity.
Look at the plot and form an opinion before computing anything: does it look clustered, evenly spread, or neither? Point pattern analysis rewards having a prior expectation, because several of the statistics are easy to misread.



Explore the pattern’s first-order properties using quadrat counts and a kernel estimate of the intensity. Does the intensity look constant across the window?














Two complementary views. One function divides the window into a grid and counts points per cell — crude
but easy to test. Another gives a smooth kernel estimate of the intensity
surface; it is the `ppp` method of a familiar function.
The bandwidth matters: too small and you see noise, too large and you smooth the
structure away.



What this shows

Two complementary views of the first-order structure — how the density of points varies across the window.
Quadrat counts are crude but directly testable. Kernel intensity is smooth and easier to look at, but the bandwidth is a choice: too small and you are looking at noise, too large and you smooth the structure away.
Neither says anything about whether points interact with one another. That is second-order structure, and it comes later.



Fit a homogeneous Poisson process, then an inhomogeneous one whose intensity depends on the coordinates. Compare them.














`ppm(ants, ~1)` fits a homogeneous Poisson process — constant intensity, points
independent. `ppm(ants, ~ x + y)` lets the log intensity vary linearly across
the window.
The second is still a Poisson process: points remain independent given the
intensity. Only the first-order structure has changed.



What this shows

The homogeneous model assumes constant intensity; the inhomogeneous one lets the log intensity vary linearly across the window.
Both are still Poisson processes, and this is the point students most often miss: in both, points are placed independently given the intensity. Only the first-order structure has changed. Neither model contains any interaction between points.



Assess the goodness of fit of both models using quadrat tests.














There is a test that compares observed and expected counts per quadrat. A small
p-value says the homogeneous Poisson model does not fit — but it will not tell
you whether the cause is a trend in intensity or genuine interaction between
points.



What this shows

A small p-value says the homogeneous Poisson model does not fit.
It does not say why. The test compares observed and expected counts per cell, so it responds to a varying intensity and to interaction between points in exactly the same way. To distinguish them you need the K-function — and even that needs care, as the envelope comparison in Q2 shows.
Note also the warning about small expected counts: the chi-squared approximation is unreliable when quadrats contain few points, which is a reason to be cautious about the exact p-value rather than just the conclusion.



Examine the second-order properties using Ripley’s \(K\)-function. Is the pattern clustered, regular, or consistent with complete spatial randomness?














`Kest()` estimates Ripley's K, and `envelope()` gives simulation bounds under
complete spatial randomness.
Above the theoretical line means clustering, below means regularity. Ant nests
compete for space, so think about which you would expect before you look.



What this shows

Ripley’s K with a simulation envelope under complete spatial randomness.
Above the theoretical curve suggests clustering, below suggests regularity or inhibition. For ant nests, competition for space and forage makes regularity the biologically plausible expectation.

title: Week 11 tutorial: Spatial point processes
text:
Challenge

Fit a model with a quadratic trend surface, using x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2) as covariates, and compare it with the linear one.














`ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))`. The `I()` is needed so `^` means power
rather than formula-crossing.
Compare with the linear-trend fit using `AIC()`. A quadratic surface can capture
a ridge or a hollow that a plane cannot.



What this shows

The quadratic trend surface can capture a ridge or a hollow in intensity that a plane cannot. Compare with the linear fit by AIC.
Be careful about what this shows: a better-fitting intensity surface tells you the points are unevenly distributed, not that they interact.



Simulate 99 point patterns from your best model and compare the resulting envelope with the observed \(K\)-function, using envelope().














The same envelope function you used in Q1 item 5 accepts a *fitted model* in place
of the point pattern, in which case it simulates from that model rather than
from complete spatial randomness. That is the sharper test: it asks whether
anything is left unexplained once the trend is accounted for.
If the observed K now sits inside the envelope, the inhomogeneity explained the
apparent clustering.



What this shows

This is the sharpest idea in the week.
The envelope is now simulated from the fitted inhomogeneous model rather than from complete spatial randomness. That changes the question from “are these points arranged as if uniform and independent?” to “is there anything left once the trend is accounted for?”.
It matters because a varying intensity alone produces more close pairs than CSR predicts, and so makes an independent pattern look clustered. Comparing against CSR confounds first-order and second-order structure. If the observed K now sits inside the envelope, the apparent clustering was inhomogeneity all along.
This confounding is the most common real error in point pattern analysis, and it is worth remembering well beyond this course.

title: Week 11 tutorial: Spatial point processes
section: Q2: real covariates, and the envelope you should be comparing against
text:
Q2: real covariates, and the envelope you should be comparing against
The ants have no measured covariates, so the trend surface above had to be built out of the coordinates themselves. This section uses a pattern that comes with covariates attached, and then makes the comparison that the lectures single out as the most common error in point pattern analysis.
bei records 3604 Beilschmiedia pendula trees in a 1000 by 500 metre plot on Barro Colorado Island, and bei.extra carries elevation (elev) and slope (grad) over the same window.

Fit a homogeneous Poisson process and then an inhomogeneous one with elevation and slope, and compare them.














The two covariates in `bei.extra` are called `elev` and `grad`.
`ppm()` takes them from `data = bei.extra`, matching them to the points by
location. The model is log-linear in the intensity, so a positive coefficient
means more trees where that covariate is higher.



What this shows

Both covariates matter, and strongly: elevation enters at 0.0214 per metre (\(z = 9.4\)) and slope at 5.85 (\(z = 22.9\)). AIC falls from 42764 to 42295, so the intensity is emphatically not constant — these trees prefer higher, steeper ground.
Take the size of the slope coefficient seriously. grad is a dimensionless gradient, mostly between 0 and 0.35 here, so moving from flat ground to the steepest parts multiplies the intensity by about \(e^{5.85 \times 0.3} \approx 5.8\). That is a first-order effect: a statement about where trees are, with no claim yet about whether they influence each other.



Now the comparison that matters. Compute the \(K\)-function envelope under CSR, and then the inhomogeneous \(K\)-function envelope under the fitted model, and read both at 10, 25 and 50 metres. What does each tell you?














For the second envelope, simulate from the **fitted model** rather than from CSR:
pass `fit.ipp` as the first argument to `envelope()`. Each simulation is then an
inhomogeneous Poisson pattern with the estimated intensity surface, and `Kinhom`
is the version of $K$ that allows for a varying intensity.
`correction = "border"` keeps the computation manageable on 3604 points.

What the CSR envelope says. The observed \(K\) is four times its upper limit at 10 m. Taken at face value that is overwhelming evidence of clustering between trees.
What the fitted envelope says. Still above, but by 2.4 times rather than 4.3, and the gap keeps closing as \(r\) grows. So a large part of what the CSR comparison called “clustering” was not interaction between trees at all: it was the trees following the terrain. Elevation and slope vary smoothly, so trees gather where conditions suit them, and a pattern with a varying intensity produces close pairs even when the points are placed completely independently of one another.
Why this is the error to avoid. Had you stopped at the CSR envelope you would have concluded that these trees cluster strongly and gone looking for a biological mechanism. Half of the apparent effect is topography, which you measured and could have accounted for. Compare against a model that contains what you already know, not against a null nobody believes.
And what is left is real. The observed curve stays outside the fitted envelope at every distance, so there is clustering beyond what elevation and slope explain — seed dispersal keeps offspring near the parent, and unmeasured soil variation does the rest. That residual is precisely what a log-Gaussian Cox process is for: it puts a Gaussian random field in the log-intensity to absorb the structure the covariates missed, instead of pretending it is not there.
A practical note: nsim = 39 gives an envelope equivalent to a 5% two-sided test. Raise it if you want a finer resolution on the p-value, and expect the computation to take proportionally longer.

title: Week 11 tutorial: Spatial point processes
text:
Week 11 complete




What you have learnt
You have analysed the third type of spatial data, where the locations themselves are the random quantity.

A different question. For geostatistical and areal data the locations are given and the values are random. For a point pattern the locations are the data, and the question is whether they are clustered, regular or random.
First-order versus second-order. Intensity is how many points per unit area and how that varies across the window; interaction is whether points attract or repel each other. They are genuinely different, and are easily confused.
Complete spatial randomness is the homogeneous Poisson process, and it is the null against which everything else is judged.
Quadrat tests are simple but blunt: a small p-value tells you the homogeneous Poisson model fails without saying whether the cause is a trend in intensity or interaction between points.
Ripley’s K with a simulation envelope separates the two. Above the theoretical curve suggests clustering, below suggests regularity.
The important subtlety. Fitting an inhomogeneous Poisson process and then re-testing with an envelope simulated from that model asks whether anything is left once the trend is accounted for. Apparent clustering often turns out to be a varying intensity rather than interaction — the classic confounding of first and second order.

title: Week 9 tutorial: Area-level data and spatial autocorrelation
text: Week 9 — Areal data and Moran’s I

title: Week 9 tutorial: Area-level data and spatial autocorrelation
text:
Overview
Weeks 7 and 8 dealt with data measured at points. From this week the data are measured over areas, and the first thing an areal analysis needs is a definition of which areas are neighbours.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

define neighbours for a set of areas, and build the corresponding weight matrix under different coding schemes;
compute and map a standardised incidence ratio; and
test for spatial autocorrelation, and say what the test does and does not tell you.


The data
scotland_lip records male lip cancer in the 56 Scottish counties, 1975–80. For each county it gives the number of cases observed and the number expected from the county’s age and sex structure, so that the comparison is between counties rather than between populations of different sizes. The covariate, aff, is the proportion of the workforce in agriculture, fishing and forestry — a proxy for time spent outdoors, and so for exposure to sunlight, which is a risk factor for lip cancer.



Column
Description




county
county name


cases
observed cases


expected
cases expected from the age and sex structure


aff
proportion employed in agriculture, fishing or forestry


sir
standardised incidence ratio, cases / expected


geometry
the county boundary



It is an sf object, so the county polygons travel with the data: there is no separate shapefile to read.

title: Week 9 tutorial: Area-level data and spatial autocorrelation
section: Q1: neighbours, weights and spatial autocorrelation
text:
Q1: neighbours, weights and spatial autocorrelation

Load the scotland_lip dataset from the course package and check that you understand what each column holds.











`data(scotland_lip)` — it is already an `sf` object, so the geometry comes with
it. Look at the columns before going on.



What this shows

An sf object: the attribute table and the county polygons together. cases and expected are the observed and expected counts, and aff is the proportion of the workforce in agriculture, fishing and forestry — a proxy for outdoor work and so for sunlight exposure.



Calculate the standardised incidence ratio (SIR) for each county, defined as observed cases divided by expected cases. Map it, and interpret what you see.














The SIR is observed over expected. There is a helper: `sir(cases, expected)`.
A value above 1 means more cases than the age-sex structure of that county would
predict. Map it with a diverging scale centred on 1, so above and below are
visually distinct.



What this shows

The SIR is observed over expected, so 1 means “as many cases as the county’s population structure predicts”.
Read the map with the next item in mind. The most extreme values tend to sit in counties with small expected counts, because an SIR based on 2 expected cases is extremely noisy — observing 4 gives an SIR of 2 with nothing unusual happening. That instability is the problem the CAR models in week 10 exist to solve.



Plot the SIR against aff. Is there a substantial association between the two, and is it in the direction you would expect?














Scatter plot of SIR against `aff`. AFF is a proxy for outdoor work and hence
sunlight exposure, which is a known risk factor for lip cancer — so a positive
slope is the expected direction.



What this shows

A weak positive association, in the direction the science predicts: more outdoor work, more sunlight, more lip cancer.
The scatter is wide, so this is suggestive rather than conclusive on its own — and note that neither the SIR nor this relationship accounts for the spatial correlation you are about to detect.



Find the neighbours of each Scottish county using Queen contiguity, and map the neighbourhood structure you obtain.














`spdep` builds a neighbour list straight from polygons. Its `queen` argument
decides the rule: `TRUE` counts a shared corner as adjacency, `FALSE` requires a
shared edge.
Scotland has islands. If a region ends up with no neighbours, that is a real
feature of the geography, not a bug — though `snap` can bridge small gaps.



What this shows

Queen contiguity treats counties sharing a corner as neighbours. The plotted network shows how the counties connect.
Three counties end up with no neighbours at all: Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles. That is not a bug — an island genuinely shares no boundary with anything. You have to decide what to do about it, and the choice affects everything downstream. Options are to allow empty sets with zero.policy = TRUE, to use a rule that always yields neighbours such as k nearest or a distance threshold, or to bridge the gap with a snapping tolerance, remembering that the tolerance is in the units of the geometry — metres here.



Which county or counties have the largest number of neighbours?














`card()` gives the number of neighbours per region. Find the maximum and which
county attains it.



What this shows

The most connected county sits in the middle of the mainland, as you would expect. Under a binary weights matrix it will exert more total influence on the statistics than a peripheral county, which is one reason row standardisation is often preferred.



Produce a map showing Wigtown and its neighbours.














Find Wigtown's index, pull its neighbours out of the neighbour list, then map
the three categories: the county itself, its neighbours, and everywhere else.



What this shows

Wigtown and its neighbours, drawn to make the adjacency concrete. It is worth tracing one county by eye like this before trusting a 56 by 56 matrix built by a function.



Construct the spatial weights matrix twice: once with binary coding, and once row-standardised, so that each row sums to one.














`nb2mat()` with `style = "B"` for binary and `style = "W"` for row-standardised.
Row-standardised means each row sums to one, so a region with many neighbours
gives each of them less weight.
Islands with no neighbours need `zero.policy = TRUE`.



What this shows

Two encodings of the same neighbour list.
Binary gives every neighbour a weight of 1, so a county with eight neighbours contributes eight units of influence and one with two contributes two.
Row-standardised divides by the number of neighbours, so every county’s neighbours carry the same total weight of 1. Check the row sums to see this.
The choice changes Moran’s I and it changes what a CAR model smooths towards. It belongs in the methods section, not left implicit.



Test for spatial autocorrelation using Moran’s \(I\). What do you conclude?














Convert the neighbour list into a weights list object first, then pass it to
the Moran's I test function.
Positive Moran's I means nearby counties have similar SIRs. Check the p-value,
but also look at the statistic against its expectation, which is -1/(n-1) rather
than zero.



What this shows

Moran’s I with a small p-value: there is strong evidence of positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning neighbouring counties have similar SIRs.
Note the expectation reported alongside the statistic. Under the null, Moran’s I is not centred on zero but on \(-1/(n-1)\). Here it prints as \(-0.0192\), which is \(-1/52\): the three island groups have no neighbours and are dropped, so the test runs on 53 counties, not 56. Compare the statistic with that figure, not with 0.
The value of the statistic depends on how you weighted the neighbours. Row standardising, as above, gives \(0.497\); the binary matrix from item 7 gives \(0.437\), which is the figure quoted in the lecture. Neither is more correct, but you should say which you used.
This result is the justification for week 10. If neighbouring counties are genuinely alike, a model can borrow strength between them — which is what makes the unstable small-area SIRs estimable.

title: Week 9 tutorial: Area-level data and spatial autocorrelation
text:
Challenge

Find the neighbours of each Scottish county using the 3 nearest neighbours, and map the neighbourhood structure obtained.














Two steps: find the k nearest centroids, then convert that to a neighbour list
with `knn2nb()`. Note this gives every region exactly three neighbours,
including the islands — which is either a feature or a distortion,
depending on what you think adjacency should mean.



What this shows

k nearest neighbours guarantees every county exactly three neighbours, islands included. That solves the empty-set problem, but at a price: adjacency is no longer symmetric in the way contiguity is, and a county can be “near” something across a substantial stretch of sea.



Find the neighbours of each Scottish county using a distance and map the neighbourhood structure obtained.














The distance-based constructor in `spdep` takes a lower and an upper bound. The geometry is in
metres, so the bounds must be too.



What this shows

A distance threshold instead. The bound is in metres, because the geometry is: d2 = 50 would be 50 metres and give every county zero neighbours. With 50 km the counties have 8.5 neighbours on average, but 9 remote counties are still isolated; at 100 km only one is isolated, but each county has about 22 neighbours. Choosing it is a modelling decision: too small and islands are isolated again, too large and everything is everyone’s neighbour.



Find the neighbours of each Scottish county using contiguity neighbours of order 2, and map the neighbourhood structure obtained.














There is a `spdep` function for higher-order (lagged) neighbours. Order 2 means "neighbours of my
neighbours", which widens the definition of local considerably.



What this shows

Second-order contiguity means neighbours of neighbours. This widens the definition of “local” considerably and will smooth more aggressively in a model.



Construct the spatial weights matrix using inverse distances as the weights.














Compute inverse distances between centroids, then pass them to `nb2mat()` via
`glist`. Closer neighbours then carry more weight than distant ones.



What this shows

Inverse-distance weights let closer neighbours count for more, rather than treating all neighbours alike. It is the most intuitively appealing scheme of the four, though it introduces a dependence on the distance units and on how centroids were computed.
Taken together, the four schemes in this Challenge make the real point of the week: there is no single correct W. Each encodes a different idea of what makes two areas neighbours, each gives different answers, and the choice must be reported and justified rather than accepted as a default.

title: Week 9 tutorial: Area-level data and spatial autocorrelation
section: Q2: a second geography, and a second statistic
text:
Q2: a second geography, and a second statistic
Everything above was done on 56 Scottish counties, where three islands had no neighbours at all and had to be handled before anything else could happen. Not every geography is like that, and it is worth seeing one that is not.
nw_obesity holds the 33 local authority districts of North West England, with the number of children measured as obese out of the number measured, and the district’s average IDACI score. It is the example from the lectures, and the one week 10 models.

Build the neighbour structure for these districts and check it. How does it compare with Scotland’s?














`poly2nb()` again — shared borders. Set the row names on the data first; given an
`sf` object it takes its names from `row.names(x)`.
`card()` gives the number of neighbours of each area.
The number you are most interested in is how many areas have none.



What this shows

Thirty-three districts, 4.42 neighbours on average, and no isolated areas — every district borders at least one other. Ribble Valley and Manchester have eight each, Warrington seven.
Compare Scotland: 56 counties, and Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles with no neighbours under any contiguity rule. The difference is not statistical, it is geographical, and it is the first thing to check when you meet a new map. A zero.policy argument you do not need is better than one you forgot.
Note also that mean neighbour counts of 4 to 5 are typical for an administrative partition of a landmass. If yours comes out at 46, as it does when a snapping tolerance is set in the wrong units, something has gone wrong with the geometry rather than with the geography.



Test the obesity proportions for spatial autocorrelation with both Moran’s I and Geary’s C, and reconcile the two answers.














The variable of interest is `prop_obese`, the proportion of children measured as
obese.
The Geary equivalent of `moran.mc()` is `geary.mc()`, with the same arguments.
Before reading the output, recall which direction each statistic moves in:
Moran's I goes **up** under positive autocorrelation, Geary's C goes **down**,
away from its null expectation of 1.



What this shows

Moran’s I is 0.2599 with \(p = 0.0073\). Geary’s C is 0.8343 with \(p = 0.099\). Both are pointing the same way — I above its null expectation of \(-1/32 = -0.031\), C below its null expectation of 1 — but only one of them clears 5%.
A note on geary.mc’s output, because the naming misleads people. It reports alternative hypothesis: greater, yet positive autocorrelation makes C small. spdep has already taken care of the direction: the p-value it prints is the probability of a C this far below 1 by chance. You do not need to switch to alternative = "less" — that would test for negative autocorrelation, and here it returns 0.90.
Why they disagree. The two statistics weight the data differently. Moran’s I is built from products of deviations from the overall mean, \((y_i-\bar y)(y_j-\bar
y)\), so it responds to broad clustering: a deprived half of the region and a less deprived half. Geary’s C is built from squared differences between neighbours, \((y_i-y_j)^2\), so it responds to local smoothness and is more affected by sharp contrasts between adjacent districts. North West England has a clear regional gradient — Merseyside and Greater Manchester against the rural north — but also some abrupt district-to-district jumps within the conurbations, and those pull C back towards 1.
What to report. Both, and the disagreement. With 33 areas neither test has much power, so a p-value of 0.0073 and one of 0.099 are not as different as they look. The defensible summary is that there is evidence of positive spatial autocorrelation, stronger at the regional scale than between immediate neighbours — which is exactly the situation a CAR model in week 10 is built to handle.

title: Week 9 tutorial: Area-level data and spatial autocorrelation
text:
Week 9 complete




What you have learnt
You have moved from point-referenced to area-level data, where “nearby” has to be defined rather than measured.

Standardised incidence ratios. Observed over expected, so a value above 1 is more cases than the population structure predicts. SIRs based on small expected counts are extremely noisy — which is exactly the problem CAR models solve next week.
Adjacency is a modelling choice. Queen or rook contiguity, k nearest neighbours, a distance threshold, or higher-order lags. Each encodes a different idea of what makes two areas neighbours, and each gives different answers.
Islands are real. Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles have no contiguous neighbours at all. You either bridge them with a snapping tolerance, use a distance or k-nearest rule, or handle empty neighbour sets explicitly.
Weights matrices. Binary treats all neighbours alike; row-standardised gives each area’s neighbours equal total influence, so an area with many neighbours weights each one less.
Moran’s I. A global test for spatial autocorrelation. Note its expectation under the null is \(-1/(n-1)\), not zero.

The point to hold on to: every one of these results depends on the weights matrix you chose. Report that choice as part of the analysis.

title: Week 7 tutorial: Exploring geostatistical data and the variogram
text: Week 7 — Geostatistics and variograms

title: Week 7 tutorial: Exploring geostatistical data and the variogram
text:
Overview
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

explore and visualise geostatistical data;
examine the association between an outcome and a covariate;
construct an empirical variogram and read the nugget, sill and range off it; and
judge whether a variogram is evidence of spatial correlation, or only of noise.


The data
The galicia data record lead concentration measured in moss at 132 sampling stations across Galicia, in north-west Spain, with a co-located measurement of airborne particulate matter. Moss takes up metals from the air, so it serves as a natural monitor of what has been deposited. These data are the running example for this week and the next.







Column
Description




lead
lead concentration


loglead
log lead concentration — this is the response you will model


long
longitude, decimal degrees


lat
latitude, decimal degrees


pm10
particulate matter under 10 micrometres



RiskMap, which you also attach below, ships a different dataset that is also called galicia. Always name the package you mean: data(galicia, package = "lsda").

title: Week 7 tutorial: Exploring geostatistical data and the variogram
section: Q1: exploring the data and building a variogram
text:
Q1: exploring the data and building a variogram

Load the galicia dataset from the course package and check that you understand what each column holds.











`data(galicia, package = "lsda")` — say `package = "lsda"`, because `RiskMap`
also ships a `galicia`, with only three columns, and loading that one instead
will break everything that follows. Five columns: the lead concentration and its
log, the coordinates, and PM10. Check which is which before you go further — you will be
modelling the log, not the raw concentration.



What this shows

Five columns: the lead concentration, its logarithm, the two coordinates and PM10. You will model loglead rather than lead, because concentrations are positive and right-skewed, and the Gaussian process the model assumes is symmetric and unbounded.



Map the lead concentration and comment on the design.














Turn the data frame into an `sf` object with `st_as_sf()`, telling it which
columns hold the coordinates and what CRS they are in (these are longitude and
latitude, so EPSG:4326).
Then map it. When you look at the map, ask where the stations are — is the
design regular, clustered, or opportunistic? That governs what you can estimate.



What this shows

The map shows where the 132 stations are, and this is worth more than a moment’s attention. The design determines what the data can support: sparse regions will have wide prediction intervals in week 8, and the near-absence of closely spaced pairs is exactly why the nugget turns out to be unidentifiable there.
Design is not a detail you inherit — if you were planning this survey, this map is what you would be choosing.



Plot log lead concentration against PM10. Is there a substantial association between the two?














An ordinary scatter plot of `loglead` against `pm10`, with a fitted line.
Both are products of traffic and industry, so a positive association would not
be surprising.



What this shows

A positive association, which is unsurprising: lead deposition and PM10 are both products of traffic and industry, so they share their sources.
This matters for the next item. Because PM10 is itself spatially organised, some of what looks like spatial correlation in lead may simply be the effect of PM10. The variogram has to be computed after removing it.



Construct a variogram for residual \(\hat{Z}\) from \[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 d(x_i) + Z_i,\] where \(Y_i\) is the log lead concentration and \(d(x_i)\) is PM\(_{10}\) at location \(x_i\). Is there evidence of spatial correlation?














Fit `lm(loglead ~ pm10)` first, then build the variogram of its **residuals** —
not of the raw response. The variogram of the response would confound spatial
structure with the trend the covariate explains.
Add a Monte Carlo envelope so you can judge whether the shape is more than noise.



What this shows

The variogram is built from the residuals of the model with the covariate, not from the raw response. That is deliberate: the variogram assumes a constant mean, and any trend left in the data shows up as increasing dissimilarity with distance and imitates spatial correlation.
Read the shape. It rises from near the origin and flattens out, which is the signature of spatial correlation: nearby residuals are alike, distant ones are not. Where it flattens is roughly the range; the height at which it flattens is the sill.
The observed curve falls outside the shaded envelope at short distances. Since the envelope is what you would see if location carried no information, that is evidence of genuine residual spatial structure — and the reason to fit a geostatistical model in week 8 rather than stopping at lm.



Now remove the covariate and build the variogram again. How does it change, and what does that tell you about what PM10 was accounting for?














Repeat with `lm(loglead ~ 1)`, that is with no covariate.
Compare the two variograms. If removing the covariate makes the variogram rise
more steeply, the covariate was explaining part of what otherwise looks like
spatial correlation.



What this shows

The same variogram with the covariate removed. It rises more steeply and further.
That difference is the point. PM10 was explaining part of the variation that now appears as spatial correlation. Fit a model without it and the spatial process has to absorb that structure instead — which is precisely what happens to the estimated covariance parameters in week 8.



Carry out a confirmatory Monte Carlo test for spatial correlation. Does it confirm what you saw in the previous two items? Vary the number of permutations: does your conclusion depend on it?














The envelope test permutes the residuals across locations many times. Under the
null of no spatial correlation, location is irrelevant, so a permuted variogram
is as good as the real one.
The observed curve lying outside the envelope at short distances is evidence of
spatial correlation. Try changing the number of permutations and see how stable
your conclusion is.



What this shows

Changing the number of permutations refines how finely the p-value is resolved — with 99 the smallest attainable is 0.01 — and reduces Monte Carlo noise, but it does not change the underlying evidence.
If your conclusion flips between 99 and 999 permutations, that is informative in itself: the result is marginal and should be reported that way rather than presented as a finding.

title: Week 7 tutorial: Exploring geostatistical data and the variogram
text:
Challenge
Using the dataset named loaloa, fit an appropriate model and examine the residuals for evidence of spatial correlation. The data come from a Loa loa prevalence survey in Cameroon and part of Nigeria: 197 villages, each with the number of people examined and the number infected, plus elevation and NDVI vegetation covariates.
Hint: repeat the steps from Q1 items 1 to 6. For what each column means, run ?lsda::loaloa — the documentation comes with the course package, so it works in the browser as well as in RStudio. Name the package: RiskMap has a loaloa too, with the same data under upper-case column names.

title: Week 7 tutorial: Exploring geostatistical data and the variogram
text:
Q2: reading variograms
A variogram is a picture you are meant to read, not just produce. This section puts three of them side by side and asks you to take numbers off them and say what each one means. They are deliberately different: one shows strong spatial correlation, one shows moderate correlation reaching a sill, and one shows essentially none.

Start with the example from the lectures. Build the empirical variogram of the NO\(_2\) residuals for Greater Manchester, with an envelope, and read off the nugget, the sill and the range.














The covariate is `road`, distance to the nearest major road. The variogram is of
the residuals, because a variogram assumes a constant mean.
When the table appears, look at the first few rows: is `obs_vari` inside
`[lower_bound, upper_bound]`, or outside it? And does `obs_vari` flatten off at
large distances, or is it still climbing at the last bin?



What this shows

Read the table from the top.
Nugget. The first bin sits at 0.77 km with a semi-variance of 0.62. Extrapolating the curve back to the origin gives something very close to zero, so the nugget here is negligible: two stations a few hundred metres apart would give almost the same reading.
Range. The curve is still rising at the last bin, 68.5 at 20.8 km. So the range is at least 20 km and the data cannot pin it down — the monitoring network is not wide enough to see where the correlation dies away. Reporting “the range is about 21 km” would be reading a limit of the design as a property of the process.
Sill. For the same reason there is no visible sill. If the curve has not levelled off, you have not seen the sill.
The envelope is the conclusion. For the first seven bins the observed semi-variance is below the lower envelope — 0.62 against 3.28, 1.27 against 3.39, and so on. Under the null that location carries no information, pairs of nearby stations should be no more alike than pairs of distant ones; they are far more alike. That is strong evidence of spatial correlation, and it is why week 8 fits a geostatistical model to these data.



Now produce the same plot for two more datasets — the Galicia lead residuals and the Liberia height-for-age residuals — and fill in a table of what you read off each one.














The Liberia covariate is `malaria_incidence_rate`.
Both datasets arrive in longitude and latitude, so they have to be projected
before distances mean anything — that is what `propose_utm()` and
`st_transform()` are doing.
For each of the two, ask the three questions in turn: where does the curve start,
where does it level off, and is it inside or outside the envelope?



What this shows

Galicia. The first usable bin is at 12 km with 0.018. The curve climbs to about 0.029 by 29 km, 0.033 by 61 km, and then wanders between 0.031 and 0.036 without going anywhere. So: sill about 0.035, reached somewhere around 60 to 80 km, and the curve sits below the envelope for the first three bins. Moderate spatial correlation, and this time a sill you can actually see.
Liberia. The curve is flat: 0.33, 0.41, 0.38, 0.44, 0.38, 0.37 … all the way out to 257 km, and every bin from the second onwards lies inside the envelope. A flat variogram inside the envelope is the picture of no spatial correlation. The sill is about 0.38 and it is reached immediately, which is another way of saying the whole of the variance is nugget.












nugget
sill
range
envelope

Galicia lead

Two warnings about reading numbers off these pictures.
A range you read by eye is not the range a model will estimate. Fitting the Galicia data in week 8 gives a Matérn scale of \(\hat\phi = 9.02\) km and a practical range of about 43 km — shorter than the 60 to 80 km the picture suggests. Read the variogram to get oriented and to decide whether to fit at all; get the numbers from the fit.
You cannot see below your shortest pair. Galicia’s first bin is at 12 km, so nothing the variogram shows can tell you what happens between 0 and 12 km — and the nugget lives entirely in that gap. In week 8 you will estimate a nugget for these data and get a confidence interval of \([0, \infty)\). This plot is the reason why.



Suppose you read a variogram that is flat from the origin and lies inside the envelope, as Liberia’s does. Give two quite different explanations for that picture, and say what you would do next in each case.

title: Week 7 tutorial: Exploring geostatistical data and the variogram
text:
Week 7 complete




What you have learnt
You have made the jump from time to space, and met the tool that detects spatial correlation.

Geostatistical data. Measurements at a finite set of locations, of a quantity that exists everywhere. That is what makes prediction at unobserved locations a sensible thing to ask for.
Design matters. Looking at the map of stations tells you what the data can support. Few close pairs means little information at short range — which will come back in week 8 when the nugget turns out to be unidentifiable.
The variogram. Half the mean squared difference between pairs, as a function of the distance between them. Rising then flattening is the signature of spatial correlation.
Always on residuals. You built the variogram from the residuals of a model with the covariate, not from the raw response. A trend left in the data looks like spatial correlation and will inflate the variogram.
Removing the covariate changed the variogram, which tells you PM10 was explaining part of what would otherwise have been attributed to space.
The Monte Carlo envelope test. Permuting values across locations destroys any spatial structure while keeping the marginal distribution. If the observed variogram sits outside the envelope, location matters.

The link back to the first half of the unit: AR(1) in time and the exponential covariance in space are the same idea with a different index.

title: Week 4 tutorial: Generalised linear mixed models
text: Week 4 — Generalised linear mixed models

title: Week 4 tutorial: Generalised linear mixed models
text:
Overview
So far the response has been continuous and roughly normal. This week it is a count, so the linear mixed model no longer applies directly. You extend it in the same way an ordinary linear model is extended to a GLM: a link function and a non-normal distribution, with the random effects still entering on the linear predictor scale.
That change has a cost. The likelihood of a generalised linear mixed model involves an integral over the random effects with no closed form, so it has to be approximated — and the approximations do not all agree. Much of this sheet is about seeing that for yourself.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

fit a GLM to repeated counts and recognise why it is not enough;
fit a Poisson GLMM with glmmPQL and with glmer;
explain why the GLMM likelihood cannot be evaluated exactly, and what PQL, Laplace and adaptive quadrature each do about it; and
say when PQL is adequate and when it is not.


The data
epil records two-week seizure counts for 59 people with epilepsy. Seizures were counted over an eight-week baseline period; patients were then randomised to progabide or placebo, and counted over four successive two-week periods. It comes with the MASS package rather than with the course package.
There are 236 rows: 59 patients by 4 periods.



Column
Description




y
seizure count in the two-week period — the response


trt
treatment, placebo or progabide


base
seizure count over the eight-week baseline


age
age in years


subject
patient identifier


period
which of the four periods, 1 to 4


lbase
centred log baseline count


lage
centred log age


V4
indicator for the fourth period



lbase and lage are the centred log versions of base and age; they are what the models below use, because centring makes the intercept interpretable.
Load it with:








help(epil) gives the full description.

title: Week 4 tutorial: Generalised linear mixed models
section: Q1: from a GLM to a generalised linear mixed model
text:
Q1: from a GLM to a generalised linear mixed model

For each placebo and treatment group, extract the epilepsy seizure counts at each period as a single vector and form a data frame with row vector containing the counts at different periods.











`epil` is already in long form. You want one column per period and one row per
patient, split by treatment group — so subset by `trt` and then reshape.



What this shows

The reshaped counts give one row per patient and one column per two-week period, separately for the placebo and treatment arms. This is the wide layout you need for the covariance and correlation matrices in the next item — the modelling later uses the long form.
Look at the counts themselves: they are small, skewed, and a few patients have very large values. That shape is what makes a Poisson model appropriate and a Gaussian one not.



Based on (1), for each group calculate the sample covariance matrix and sample correlation matrix.














`cov()` and `cor()` on each group's matrix of counts. Compare the two: is the
within-patient correlation similar in the placebo and treatment arms?



What this shows

The correlation matrices are the point. Within a patient, seizure counts across the four periods are strongly and fairly uniformly correlated — a patient who seizes often in one period does so in all of them.
That is not a nuisance to be removed; it is real biological variation in susceptibility between patients. Ignoring it, as the GLM in item 5 does, treats each of the four periods as four independent pieces of evidence when they are much closer to one.



Based on (1), for each group produce a pairwise scatter plot. Report your finding.


















`pairs()` on each group. Counts are skewed, so the clouds will look quite unlike
the tidy ellipses you saw for the cattle weights.



What this shows

The pairwise plots show the same thing as the correlation matrices, in a form where the skewness is visible too. Compare these clouds with the tidy ellipses of the cattle weights in week 1: count data are not symmetric, and a few patients sit far out on every axis at once.



Consider a Poisson GLM applied to the epil dataset to analyse the effect of treatment on seizure counts. Assume the seizure count follows a Poisson distribution with mean \(\lambda\), where

\[
\log(\lambda) = \eta
\] \[
\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{lbase}) + \beta_2 (\text{trt}) + \beta_3 (\text{lbase} \times \text{trt}) + \beta_4 (\text{lage}) + \beta_5 (\text{period}).
\]
Which of these covariates are statistically significant? Interpret your results.













A Poisson GLM is `glm(..., family = poisson)`. The link is log by default, so
each coefficient is a log rate ratio: `exp(coef)` is the multiplicative effect on
the expected seizure count.
The interaction `lbase * trt` asks whether the treatment effect depends on the
baseline rate.



What this shows

Read the coefficients as log rate ratios: exp(coef) is the multiplicative effect on the expected count. The coefficient on lbase is close to 1, meaning the seizure rate is roughly proportional to the baseline rate, which is what you would hope.
Now look at the residual deviance against its degrees of freedom, and at the chi-squared p-value computed underneath. The deviance is far larger than the degrees of freedom, so the model fits badly: there is much more variation than a Poisson with these covariates allows.
There are two possible causes and this test cannot separate them — genuine overdispersion, or the correlation within patients that the model is ignoring. Item 6 addresses the second.



In Question (4) above, if the variable Period is treated as a factor with four levels, use the model to refit the data. Observe if each time period has a significant effect and interpret your results.














Wrap `period` in `factor()` so each of the four periods gets its own coefficient
instead of assuming a straight-line trend in period number.



What this shows

Treating period as a factor lets each of the four periods take its own effect instead of forcing a straight line in period number. It costs two extra parameters.
The deviance barely improves, which says the linear-in-period assumption was not the problem. That is useful negative information: the misfit is not about the shape of the time trend.



Reconsider Questions (4) and (5), but this time use GLMM (PQL approach) to analyse the data, incorporating a random intercept.














`MASS` provides a penalised quasi-likelihood fitter for GLMMs. Give it a
random intercept per patient. This adds a
patient-specific intercept, so patients who seize more often than the model
expects are accounted for rather than inflating the apparent precision.
Compare the standard errors with the GLM: what happened, and why?



What this shows

The random intercept is the substantive change. Each patient now has their own baseline rate, so patients who simply seize more than their covariates predict are accounted for rather than inflating the apparent evidence.
Two things to compare with the GLM in item 5.
The standard errors are larger, particularly for the between-patient covariates such as trt. Ignoring the clustering had overstated how much independent information the data carried.
The random intercept standard deviation is substantial. That is the between-patient variation in susceptibility, and it is exactly what the Poisson GLM had to absorb as overdispersion.
One more point about interpretation. A GLMM coefficient is subject-specific: it compares the same patient under two covariate values. The GEE you meet next week estimates a population-averaged effect instead, and for a non-linear link the two are genuinely different quantities.

title: Week 4 tutorial: Generalised linear mixed models
section: Q2: a binary response, and how the likelihood is approximated
text:
Q2: a binary response, and how the likelihood is approximated
The epilepsy response is a count, and for counts the approximations below behave well. Binary responses are the hard case, and they are what you meet next week, so it is worth seeing the difference here.
The ichs data in the course package record whether each of 250 preschool children had a respiratory infection at each of six visits, together with their vitamin A status. Six binary observations per child is very little information per cluster — exactly where penalised quasi-likelihood is known to struggle.

Fit a logistic GLMM for respiratory infection on time, age, gender and vitamin A status, with a random intercept per child, using penalised quasi-likelihood. Report the estimated effect of vitamin A deficiency and the between-child standard deviation.














The same fitter as Q1 item 6: `glmmPQL()` from `MASS`. A random intercept per child
is `random = ~ 1 | id`. The response is 0/1, so `family = binomial`.
Read two things off the output: the `vitAdeficient` row of the coefficient
table, and the random-intercept standard deviation above it.



What this shows

PQL puts the vitamin A coefficient at about 0.48 on the log-odds scale, with a between-child standard deviation of about 2.33.
That standard deviation is large. On the logit scale a value of 2.33 means children differ enormously in their underlying susceptibility — far more than the covariates explain. Keep both numbers; the next item refits the same model by a better approximation and you will compare.
Note the interpretation. Because the random intercept is held fixed, \(\exp(0.48) \approx 1.6\) is the odds ratio for a given child — the subject-specific effect. Next week’s GEE answers a different question about the same data.



Refit the same model by Laplace approximation and then by adaptive Gaussian quadrature with 25 points, and compare all three sets of estimates. Which differences matter, and what do they tell you about PQL?














`lme4::glmer()` fits a GLMM by Laplace approximation, which is `nAGQ = 1`.
Adaptive Gaussian quadrature with more points is a strictly better
approximation to the same likelihood — ask for 25 of them.
The random effect is written `(1 | id)` in `lme4`'s formula syntax.
Compare the vitamin A row across the three columns, and then the two
log-likelihoods.



What this shows

The vitamin A coefficient goes 0.477 (PQL), 0.633 (Laplace), 0.604 (AGQ), and the between-child standard deviation goes 2.33, 2.72, 2.84.
PQL is the odd one out, and it is smaller on both. This is the attenuation the lectures warned about: PQL replaces the binary response by a working linear model, and with only six 0/1 observations per child that approximation is poor. It shrinks the fixed effect by about a fifth and understates the between-child variation. For the Poisson counts in Q1 the same method would have been fine — it is the combination binary response, small cluster that breaks it.
Laplace and AGQ are approximating the same likelihood, so compare their log-likelihoods: -672.3 against -666.4. Six log-likelihood units is not a rounding difference. Laplace is a one-point quadrature rule, and one point is not enough here; if the two had agreed, one point would have been enough and there would be nothing to gain from the extra work.
The practical rule: use quadrature for binary responses when you can, check that adding points stops changing the answer, and treat PQL estimates of variance components as a lower bound.
Carry the AGQ number forward. Next week you will fit the same data by GEE and get about 0.28 for vitamin A — less than half. Neither is wrong; they estimate different things, and week 5 is about which one answers your question.

title: Week 4 tutorial: Generalised linear mixed models
text:
Week 4 complete




What you have learnt
You have moved from Gaussian responses to counts, and from GLMs to GLMMs.

Why a GLM is not enough. Fitting a Poisson GLM to repeated seizure counts treats all 236 observations as independent when they come from 59 patients. The estimates may be reasonable; the standard errors are not.
The exponential family and the log link. For a Poisson model each coefficient is a log rate ratio, so exp(coef) is a multiplicative effect on the expected count.
Factor versus numeric time. Treating period as a factor lets each period have its own effect instead of assuming a straight line in period number — a weaker and often more honest assumption.
GLMMs by penalised quasi-likelihood. Adding a patient-specific random intercept accounts for patients who simply seize more than the covariates predict. Notice what happened to the standard errors.
Subject-specific interpretation. Unlike the GEE you meet next week, a GLMM coefficient describes a change for a given patient, not for the population average. For a non-linear link those are genuinely different quantities.

title: Week 2 tutorial: Linear mixed models
text: Week 2 — Linear mixed models

title: Week 2 tutorial: Linear mixed models
text:
Overview
Week 1 showed that measurements on the same subject are correlated. The linear mixed model is the first tool for doing something about it: a random effect \(\mathbf{b}_i\) lets each subject have its own intercept and slope, and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) describes what correlation is left over within a subject once that is accounted for.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

write a linear mixed model in matrix form and say what each matrix holds;
fit one with lme(), choosing a structure for \(\mathbf{R}_i\);
compare covariance structures with likelihood ratio tests and information criteria; and
interpret the fitted fixed effects and variance components.


The data
fev1 records lung function growth in 299 school-age girls from Topeka, Kansas, followed as part of the Six Cities Study of Air Pollution and Health. Each girl was enrolled at around age 6 to 10 and measured roughly annually, but at ages of her own: the number of observations per girl ranges from 1 to 12, so the data are unbalanced and there is no grid of common time points. There are 1993 measurements in all.



Column
Description




id
identifier for each girl


age
age at measurement, years


ht
height at measurement, metres


baseage, baseht
age and height at the first visit


fev1
forced expiratory volume in one second, litres


logfev1
log of fev1


logfev1_ht
log(fev1/ht), the response modelled here

title: Week 2 tutorial: Linear mixed models
section: Q1: fitting and comparing linear mixed models
text:
Q1: fitting and comparing linear mixed models
For the fev1 data, consider a linear mixed model of the form \[
\log\left( \frac{\text{FEV}_1}{\text{Height}} \right)_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Age}_{ij} + b_{0i} + b_{1i} \text{Age}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\] where

\(\log\left( \frac{\text{FEV}_1}{\text{Height}} \right)_{ij}\): the response for individual \(i\) at time \(j\);
\(\beta_0\): fixed intercept;
\(\beta_1\): fixed slope for age;
\(b_{0i}\): random intercept for individual \(i\), capturing between-subject variation;
\(b_{1i}\): random slope for age for individual \(i\);
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\): within-subject residual error.

Note that \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) and \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}_i)\).

Express the above model in matrix form and explain the corresponding matrices/vectors.
In R, use the function lme() to analyse the data by specifying \(\mathbf{G}\) as general covariance structure and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) as
2.1. independent covariance structure,
2.2. compound symmetry covariance structure,
2.3. AR(1) structure,
2.4. ARMA(1,1) structure,
where the option method in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. Select the best structure of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) in terms of the resulting AIC or BIC value.











`groupedData()` first: it tells `nlme` which column identifies the subject, so
`logfev1_ht ~ age | id`.
Then one `lme()` per structure. The mean model and `random =` stay the same
throughout — only `correlation =` changes. The four structures you need all have constructors in `nlme` whose names begin
`cor`. Independence is the absence of a `correlation` argument; for the other
three see `?corClasses`. ARMA needs both its orders given.
Use `method = "ML"`, because you are about to compare models that differ in
their fixed or covariance structure.



What this shows

Four models differing only in correlation. update() avoids retyping the call, so the one thing that changes stays visible.
The two sets of fixed effects printed at the end are almost identical. Changing the assumed error correlation barely moves the estimates; it moves the standard errors. That is the same lesson GEE makes explicit in week 5.
One thing worth knowing, because it will bite you if you try it. The question specifies a random intercept and a random slope, but fitting random = ~ age | id together with corAR1 or corARMA fails to converge on these data. That is not a bug in your code: a random slope already makes the marginal correlation change with the gap between visits, and AR(1) errors do the same thing, so the two compete to explain the same structure and the likelihood has no well-identified maximum. Comparing R_i structures with the simpler G, then choosing G afterwards, avoids the problem — which is exactly why the tutorial splits the selection into two stages.


Spot the problem. One of the four models below should not have been fitted in this form. When you compare them, look closely at compound symmetry against independence, and explain what you see. Think about what covariance structure a random intercept produces on its own.













`AIC()` and `BIC()` both accept several fitted models at once and return a table.
Lower is better for both. If they disagree, remember BIC penalises extra
parameters harder.



What this shows

Both criteria are shown because they can disagree. Here they do not: AR(1) wins decisively on each, by around 400 units of AIC over independence. A gap that large is not a close call.
That result makes sense. The girls are measured roughly annually over several years, and residuals a year apart should be more alike than residuals five years apart, which is what AR(1) allows.
The problem to spot. Compound symmetry has exactly the same log-likelihood as independence, and an AIC exactly 2 higher: the penalty for one extra parameter that bought nothing. Its fitted correlation is 0. This is not because compound symmetry is the wrong shape for these data. A random intercept already gives compound symmetry, since \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{Y}_i) = \sigma_b^2 \mathbf{J} + \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}\) (lecture, week 2). Adding corCompSymm on top asks for the same structure twice, so the random intercept absorbs all of it and the extra correlation has nothing left to explain. Fitting gls(..., correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id)) with no random effects gives the same log-likelihood again. The fair comparison for compound symmetry is therefore fit_ind itself.



With the selected structure for \(\mathbf{R}_i\), select the best structure for \(\mathbf{G}\) among the candidates below:
3.1. independent covariance structure,
3.2. diagonal covariance structure,
3.3. general covariance structure.
Again, the option method in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method.














Same idea as item 3, but now `correlation =` is held at whatever you selected
and `random =` is what varies.
The three candidates are constructors whose names begin `pd` — see
`?pdClasses`. One forces equal variances and no covariance, one allows unequal
variances but still no covariance, and the general case is `nlme`'s default when
you write `random = ~ age | id`.



What this shows

correlation is now fixed at AR(1) and random varies. The three G structures are nested: identity within diagonal within general.
Note control = lmeControl(opt = "optim"). With the default optimiser the general structure does not converge; switching optimisers fixes it. If a mixed model fails to converge, changing the optimiser is worth trying before concluding the model is wrong — though if several optimisers fail, that is a genuine signal of over-parameterisation.
In the printed variance components, pdDiag gives a standard deviation for the intercept and one for age but no correlation between them, because a diagonal G assumes that correlation is zero rather than estimating it.















Compare the three G structures the same way you compared the R structures.



What this shows

The same comparison for the between-subject structure.
Read this cautiously. A criterion ranks models; it does not tell you a parameter is real. If the general structure wins narrowly, check whether the extra covariance it estimates has a confidence interval that excludes zero before claiming girls who start higher also grow faster.



For your overall best model, interpret the parameters of the model.



































































`summary()` on the winning fit. Read three things: the fixed effects (what is
the average growth rate?), the random effects table (how much do girls differ in
intercept and slope?), and the residual standard deviation.
Try to state each in a sentence about lung function, not about the model.



What this shows

The summary is the payoff. Three things to read.
Fixed effects. The coefficient on age is the population-average annual change in log(FEV1/height). It is positive, which is lung function growing through adolescence, as it should.
Random effects. The between-girl standard deviations, compared with the residual standard deviation below them. If the intercept SD is comparable to or larger than the residual SD, girls differ from one another about as much as a single girl varies between visits — which is what makes the mixed model worthwhile.
Correlation structure. The estimated AR(1) parameter Phi. A value well above zero says residuals remain related from one visit to the next even after the random effects have absorbed the between-girl differences.
When you write this up, state each of these in a sentence about lung function rather than about the model.

title: Week 2 tutorial: Linear mixed models
section: Q2: correlation structures when the times are not a grid
text:
Q2: correlation structures when the times are not a grid
Everything above was fitted to 60 cattle weighed on the same eleven days, where corAR1() indexes observations 1 to 11 and \(\rho^{|j-k|}\) means what you expect. This section repeats the exercise on data with no common time points, where that reading of AR(1) is not available.
The cd4 data hold CD4+ counts for 369 men around HIV seroconversion, between 1 and 12 observations each, at 1342 distinct times. Weeks 2 and 3 model \(\sqrt{\text{CD4}}\), which stabilises the variance of a count-like response.

Fit a random intercept model for \(\sqrt{\text{CD4}}\) on time, then add compound symmetry to it, and compare the two. What has the second model bought?














A random intercept is `random = ~ 1 | subject`.
Compound symmetry as an error correlation is `corCompSymm()`.
Before you run it, predict what will happen: what marginal correlation does a
random intercept already induce between two observations on the same man?



What this shows

The log-likelihood is -7275.77 for both, to two decimal places. The second model has one more parameter and has bought precisely nothing, so its AIC is exactly two worse: 14559.54 against 14561.54.
This is not a numerical accident and it is worth being sure you can explain it. A random intercept already makes every pair of observations on the same man equally correlated, with \[\mbox{Corr}(Y_{ij}, Y_{ik}) = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{\sigma_b^2+\sigma^2},\] which is compound symmetry. Adding corCompSymm on top asks the model to explain the same exchangeable correlation a second time. The two parameters are not separately identifiable, and the fit lands wherever it started.
The practical rule: a random intercept and compound symmetry are two names for one structure. Use one or the other, never both.



Now replace compound symmetry with a correlation that decays with the time gap. Does that buy anything, and why could you not have used corAR1() here?














`corCAR1()` is the continuous-time version of AR(1): it uses
$\mbox{Corr} = \phi^{|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|}$ with the *actual* times, so the gaps need
not be equal and need not be integers.
`corAR1()` would use the position of the observation in the sequence instead —
first, second, third — which treats a two-week gap and a two-year gap as the
same thing.
The last line prints the estimated $\phi$.



What this shows




model

AIC

The same one extra parameter that bought nothing as compound symmetry buys 84 log-likelihood units as a continuous AR(1), and AIC falls by 166. The difference between the two is only what the parameter is attached to: a constant correlation between all pairs, or a correlation that decays with the gap.
So the data say there is serial correlation here, over and above the men simply differing from each other. \(\hat\phi = 0.159\), and the correlation between two residuals a time \(u\) apart is \(0.159^{u}\) with \(u\) in years: about 0.16 at one year, 0.03 at two. It is short-range, which is why the random intercept alone could not represent it — that term is the same at every lag.
Why not corAR1(). It would raise the correlation to the power of the difference in position, so the gap between a man’s first and second visit would count as “one” whether it was three months or three years. With 1342 distinct times that is meaningless. corCAR1() reads the times from form = ~ time | subject and uses them.
The general lesson, which the cattle data hid: with equally spaced observations corAR1() and corCAR1() agree, and you can be careless. With unequal spacing only one of them is defensible.

title: Week 2 tutorial: Linear mixed models
text:
Week 2 complete




What you have learnt
You have fitted linear mixed models and chosen between covariance structures.

Two sources of within-subject correlation. Shared random effects (\(\mathbf{Z}_i \mathbf{G} \mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\)) and serial correlation in the errors (\(\mathbf{R}_i\)). The marginal covariance is their sum.
Structures for \(\mathbf{R}_i\). Independence, compound symmetry (all pairs equally correlated), AR(1) (geometric decay with the gap) and ARMA(1,1). The choice is a claim about how correlation behaves over time, not a technicality.
Structures for \(\mathbf{G}\). Identity, diagonal and general — increasingly permissive about how subjects vary in intercept and slope, and whether those two are related.
Choosing between them with AIC and BIC, remembering that BIC penalises extra parameters harder, so the two can disagree.
Interpretation. A fitted mixed model tells you both the population average trajectory and how much individuals depart from it.

Worth trying: run_app("cov_explorer") to see what each structure actually looks like as a matrix and as simulated trajectories.
