title: Week 1 tutorial: Introduction to longitudinal data
text:
Overview
This first sheet is about looking at longitudinal data before modelling any of it. Everything you do here — the spaghetti plot, the correlation matrix, the pairwise scatter plots — is there to show you the one feature that makes these data different from anything in a first regression course: measurements on the same subject are correlated, and ignoring that is a mistake.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

load a longitudinal dataset and describe its shape, including whether it is balanced;
draw and read a spaghetti plot;
compute and interpret the mean profile, the covariance matrix and the correlation matrix over time; and
compare groups graphically, and say what a difference in profiles looks like.


The data
Two datasets are used.
cattle is a growth experiment: 60 animals were randomised to two treatment groups of 30, put out to pasture, and weighed on the same eleven occasions two weeks apart. Because every animal was weighed on every occasion, the design is balanced, and the data are stored in wide form — one row per animal.



Column
Description




group
treatment group, 0 or 1


t1 … t11
bodyweight in kg at each of the eleven occasions



fev1 is the contrasting case, introduced in Q2: an observational study in which girls were measured at ages of their own, so the data are unbalanced and stored in long form — one row per measurement.

title: Week 1 tutorial: Introduction to longitudinal data
section: Q1: describing a balanced longitudinal dataset
text:
Q1: describing a balanced longitudinal dataset

Load the cattle data from the course package and check its shape: how many animals, and how many measurements on each?











The datasets come with the course package rather than as files, so you want
`data()`, not `read.table()`. Afterwards, `dim()` and `head()` tell you the
shape and the first few rows.



What this shows

60 rows and 12 columns: one row per animal, the first column the treatment group and the remaining eleven the weights. Every animal has all eleven, so the design is balanced — which is what lets us treat the data as a 60 by 11 matrix at all.



Generate a spaghetti plot for the cattle data.














`cattle` is in wide format: one row per animal, one column per time. So a
"spaghetti plot" means drawing one line per row.
Start the plot with the first animal using `type = "l"`, then add the rest in a
loop with `lines()`. Set `ylim` from the whole dataset so no trajectory is cut
off, and remember column 1 is the group indicator, not a weight.



What this shows

Each line is one animal. Two things are worth noticing. Weight increases steadily for everyone, so there is a clear time trend. And the lines stay roughly parallel: animals that start heavy stay heavy. That persistent ordering is the within-subject correlation, and it is why treating these 660 measurements as independent would be wrong.



Calculate the sample means for observations at each time point. Additionally, compute the sample covariance matrix and sample correlation matrix.














All three summaries operate on the weight columns only, so drop the group
column first with `cattle[, -1]`.
`sapply()` applies `mean` down each column; `cov()` and `cor()` take the whole
matrix at once.



What this shows

The means rise steadily with time, as the plot suggested.
In the correlation matrix, read along any row. Correlation is high next to the diagonal — adjacent times are near 0.9 — and falls away as the gap widens, down to around 0.5 between the first and last times. That decay with lag is the pattern AR(1) is built for, and it is why compound symmetry, which forces every pair to share one correlation, would fit these data badly.



Create a pairwise scatter plot for the cattle data. Analyse and describe the key features of the observed correlations.














`pairs()` draws the full scatterplot matrix in one call. Again, exclude the
group column.
Look along the diagonals: how does the spread change as the gap between two time
points grows?



What this shows

Four times are shown rather than all eleven, because an 11 by 11 grid of panels is unreadable. The panels for adjacent times are tight, near-linear clouds; those for widely separated times are much more diffuse. This is the same information as the correlation matrix, seen directly.



Divide the cattle dataset into two groups, Group A and Group B. For each group, determine the sample means at each time point, as well as the sample covariance and sample correlation.














`which(cattle[, 1] == 0)` gives the row numbers for one group. Use that to
subset, then repeat everything from item 4 on each group separately.
Two plots side by side is `par(mfcol = c(1, 2))`.



What this shows

Group A starts heavier. By the last time point the two groups have converged and crossed over, so the difference between them is not constant — it changes with time. A model with only a group effect could not represent that; you need an interaction between group and time, which is what you fit in week 3.



Produce pairwise scatter plots for each group. Identify and discuss any similarities or differences between the two groups evident in the plots.














You already have the two group subsets from item 6, so this is `pairs()` twice.
Give each a `main` title so you can tell them apart.



What this shows

The correlation structure looks similar in both groups: the same tightening near the diagonal and loosening away from it. That matters for modelling, because it means one covariance structure can reasonably be assumed to hold for both groups rather than fitting each separately.



Plot the sample means of both groups against time within a single figure. Provide your interpretations and conclusions drawn from the figure.














Plot the first group's means with `plot()`, then add the second with `lines()`
in a different colour. Both means are vectors of length 11 that you computed in
item 6.



What this shows

The two mean curves cross. Group A is heavier at first, its growth flattens after about time 4, and group B overtakes it. This crossing is the treatment effect, and it is a difference in slope rather than in level.

title: Week 1 tutorial: Introduction to longitudinal data
section: Q2: an unbalanced dataset, measured at times of its own
text:
Q2: an unbalanced dataset, measured at times of its own
You will now work with longitudinal data on lung function growth in school-age girls from Topeka, Kansas, collected as part of the Six Cities Study of Air Pollution and Health. The dataset contains repeated pulmonary function measurements from 299 girls, typically enrolled around ages 6-10 and followed annually until high school graduation or loss to follow-up. The number of observations per individual ranges from 1 to 12, making the dataset unbalanced with respect to age.
At each visit, lung function was measured using simple spirometry, and the outcome of interest is the logarithm of the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) to height, i.e., log(FEV1/height).
The dataset is available in the course package.
Key variables include:

id: unique identifier for each girl
ht: height (m)
age: age at measurement (years)
baseht: height at the first visit
baseage: age at the first visit
fev1: volume of air exhaled in the first second (litres)
logfev1: logarithm of fev1
logfev1_ht: pre-computed log(fev1/height)


Load the dataset and check the structure of the data. How many observations are there in total? How many individuals?














`fev1` is in long format: one row per visit, not per girl. So `nrow()` is the
number of observations, and the number of girls is the number of distinct `id`
values.



What this shows

1993 observations from 299 girls — about 6.7 visits each on average, but that average conceals a lot, as the next item shows.



Summarise the number of observations per individual. What does this tell you about the balance of the data?














Count the rows per `id`, then summarise those counts. A histogram of them shows
the shape of the follow-up.
If every girl had the same count, the data would be balanced — what do you see?



What this shows

The distribution is right-skewed. Most girls have several visits, but some have only one or two. So the data are unbalanced: \(n_i\) differs between girls.
This is not a defect and does not need fixing. It does have two consequences. The design matrices differ in size between girls, so the model has to be written per subject. And a girl with two visits carries far less information than one with twelve, which is exactly what produces shrinkage in the week 3 predictions.



Produce a plot of log(fev1 / height) against age for 50 randomly selected girls. Connect points for the same individual. Comment on the variability between individuals and the measurement patterns over age.














Draw a random sample of `id` values first, then keep only the rows belonging to
them. In `ggplot`, `group = id` is what stops the lines being joined into one
long zigzag across girls.
Set a seed so your plot is reproducible.



What this shows

The spaghetti plot for the unbalanced case. Compared with the cattle data, notice that the lines start and stop at different ages and have different numbers of points — that is the imbalance made visible.
There is substantial variation between girls in both level and slope, which is the motivation for allowing a random intercept and a random slope in week 2.



Compute and plot the average log(fev1 / height) at each age, aggregating across individuals.














Group by `age` and take the mean of `logfev1_ht` within each. Plotting the
result gives the population-average growth curve.
Ages are not on a common grid, so some ages are supported by very few girls —
worth bearing in mind when you read the plot.



What this shows

Averaging within each age gives the population-level growth curve, which rises steadily through adolescence.
Ages were rounded before averaging because girls were not measured on a common grid; without rounding, most ages would be supported by a single girl. Even so the extremes are based on few observations, so treat the ends of the curve with caution.

title: Week 1 tutorial: Introduction to longitudinal data
section: Q3: when there are no common time points at all
text:
Q3: when there are no common time points at all
The cattle were weighed on the same eleven days and the Topeka girls attended at ages that differ between girls. There is a third case, and it is the most common one in practice: every subject is measured at times of its own, so no two subjects share a time point at all.
The cd4 data in the course package hold CD4+ cell counts for men enrolled in a study of HIV seroconversion. time is measured in years, with zero at seroconversion, so it runs negative before and positive after.

Establish what kind of design this is. How many subjects are there, how many observations does each contribute, and how many distinct observation times appear in the file?














`table()` on the subject identifier counts the rows belonging to each man, so
its minimum, median and maximum describe how uneven the design is.
For the second part, count the distinct values of `time`, and then ask how many
subjects share the single most popular one. Compare that with the 60 cattle who
all shared eleven days.



What this shows

2376 rows, 369 men, and between 1 and 12 visits each with a median of 6. So the design is unbalanced in the same way the FEV1 data were.
The second line is the new part. There are 1342 distinct times among 2376 observations, and the most popular single time is shared by just 25 men. There is essentially no common grid at all.
That breaks a tool you used in Q1 without thinking about it. “The sample mean at each time point” was a sensible summary for 60 cattle weighed on the same eleven days. Here it would give you over a thousand means, most of them averages of one or two observations. The same applies to the sample covariance matrix across times: there is no matrix to form.



Draw the individual trajectories, and add a summary of the average pattern that does not depend on subjects sharing time points. What does the average CD4+ trajectory do around seroconversion?














`lowess()` is a scatterplot smoother: it estimates the mean of `y` as a smooth
function of `x` without needing repeated values of `x`. It returns a list with
components `x` and `y`, already sorted, ready for `lines()`.
The dashed vertical line marks seroconversion. Look at what the smoother does to
the left of it and to the right.



What this shows

The grey lines are the spaghetti plot you already know. What is new is how the average was obtained: a smoother, not a mean per time point, because there are no time points to take means at.
The picture itself is the well-known one. Counts are roughly flat before seroconversion, fall steeply across it, and then decline more slowly. Individual trajectories are wildly variable around that average and cross each other freely.
Two things to take away for the modelling weeks.
The between-subject spread is large — the grey lines occupy a wide band at every time — so a model without a subject-specific term will not describe these data.
The counts are strongly right-skewed and bounded below by zero, running from 10 to over 3000. Weeks 2 and 3 model \(\sqrt{\text{CD4}}\) rather than the raw count for that reason; it is a variance-stabilising transformation for something that behaves roughly like a count.

title: Week 1 tutorial: Introduction to longitudinal data
text:
Week 1 complete




What you have learnt
You have worked with two longitudinal datasets and seen the feature that motivates the whole unit: observations on the same subject are not independent.

A spaghetti plot shows every subject’s trajectory at once. Lines that stay ordered — heavy animals staying heavy — are correlation you can see by eye.
The sample correlation matrix over time puts a number on it. Correlation was strong between adjacent times and decayed as the gap widened. That decay is what AR(1) will model in week 2.
Balanced and unbalanced designs. The cattle data are balanced: every animal measured at the same 11 times. The FEV1 data are not — girls contribute between 1 and 12 visits at ages that do not line up. That difference changes what the design matrices look like and which methods are convenient.
Group comparisons. Splitting by treatment and comparing means over time is the crudest form of the analysis the rest of the unit does properly.

The thing to carry forward: if you analysed either dataset with ordinary linear regression, you would be assuming away the correlation you have just spent an hour looking at. The standard errors would be wrong.

title: Week 3 tutorial: Inference for linear mixed models
text: Week 3 — Estimation and inference

title: Week 3 tutorial: Inference for linear mixed models
Week 3 tutorial: Inference for linear mixed models
section: Q1: choosing, fitting and checking a linear mixed model
text:
Q1: choosing, fitting and checking a linear mixed model
For the cattle data, use the linear mixed model with random intercept and random slope in Day: to model the bodyweight growth of cattle over the observation period, where \(\mathbf{b}_i\)=\((b_{i1},b_{i2})'\sim N_2(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) with \(\mathbf{G}\) being (\(2\times 2\)) positive definite and \(\varepsilon_i=(\varepsilon_{i1},...,\varepsilon_{i11})'\sim
N_{11}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}_i)\) with \(\mathbf{R}_i\) being (\(11\times
11\)) positive definite.










`groupedData()` needs the response, the time variable and the subject
identifier: `Y ~ day | subject`. The cattle data are wide, so you will need to
reshape to long form first.



What this shows

reshape() turns the 60 by 11 wide matrix into 660 rows, one per animal per day. groupedData() then records that subject identifies the clusters, which is what lets nlme know which rows belong together.



Express the above model in matrix form and explain the corresponding matrices/vectors.
In R, use the function lme() to analyse the data by specifying \(\mathbf{G}\) as general covariance structure and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) as
2.1. independent covariance structure,














The independent structure is the default: give `lme()` no `correlation`
argument at all. Use a random intercept only (`~ 1 | subject`) for now; the
random slope comes back when you compare structures for G in item 3.



What this shows

The four fixed effects are the intercept, the growth rate, the group difference in level, and the group difference in slope — the interaction, which is the parameter the experiment exists to estimate.
Note the random intercept only at this stage. The question specifies a random slope as well, and you will add it in item 3, when you choose a structure for \(\mathbf{G}\). Comparing R_i structures with the simpler G first is deliberate: with a random slope, ARMA(1,1) does not converge on these data, because a random slope already makes the marginal correlation depend on the gap between days and an ARMA error does the same thing. The two compete to explain one feature, and the likelihood has no clear maximum.


2.2. compound symmetry covariance structure,
Spot the problem. Before you run this, predict the estimated correlation. You met the same situation in week 2: what covariance structure does lme.ide, with its random intercept, already imply?













`update()` saves retyping the whole call — pass only what changes.
Compound symmetry means every pair of times is equally correlated, however far
apart. The `nlme` constructor for it is listed in `?corClasses`; its `form`
argument names the grouping, here `~ 1 | subject`.



What this shows

The problem to spot. The estimated correlation is 0, and in the comparison below lme.cs has exactly the same log-likelihood as lme.ide (\(-2634.935\)), with an AIC exactly 2 higher: the penalty for a parameter that bought nothing. This is the same trap as week 2. A random intercept already makes the marginal covariance compound symmetric, so corCompSymm has nothing left to explain. In this comparison, compound symmetry is really represented by lme.ide itself.


2.3. AR(1) structure,













Now correlation should decay with the gap in days rather than being constant —
an autoregressive structure of order 1. Its `form` needs the time variable as
well as the grouping, so `~ day | subject`.



What this shows

The AR(1) parameter. Correlation between residuals now decays as \(\rho^{|s-t|}\), so adjacent days are strongly related and distant days barely so — a much more plausible story for growth measurements than one constant correlation.


2.4. ARMA(1,1) structure,
where the option method in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. Select the best structure of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) in terms of the resulting AIC or BIC value.













The ARMA constructor needs both orders given explicitly, `p` and `q`.
`AIC()` and `BIC()` each accept several fitted models and return one row per
model; lower is better. Use them rather than `anova()`: the likelihood ratio
tests `anova()` prints assume each model is nested in the next, and compound
symmetry and AR(1) are not nested.



What this shows

AIC() and BIC() compare the four fits without needing them to be nested. anova() would print the same criteria plus likelihood ratio tests between adjacent rows, but compound symmetry and AR(1) are not nested (neither is a special case of the other), so those \(p\)-values would be meaningless.
AR(1) and ARMA(1,1) both improve enormously on independence and compound symmetry — around 440 units of AIC. Between the two the difference is small: ARMA edges it on both criteria, but by about 7 units of AIC and only 2 of BIC, which is close to a tie.
Here you meet a practical constraint that model selection tables do not show. ARMA(1,1) cannot be fitted alongside the richer G structures you are about to compare, so continuing with it would mean abandoning the second stage entirely. AR(1) is chosen for that reason, and because BIC separates the two by almost nothing. That is a defensible decision, but it is a decision, and it belongs in the write-up rather than being made silently.



With the selected structure for \(\mathbf{R}_i\), select the best structure for \(\mathbf{G}\) among the candidates below:
3.1. independent covariance structure,














Now hold `correlation` fixed and vary `random`. The most restrictive option forces the random intercept and slope to have equal
variance and zero covariance. Look for the `pd` constructor meaning "identity".



What this shows

Now the random slope appears. pdIdent is the most restrictive G: equal variances for intercept and slope, and no covariance between them.
control = lmeControl(opt = "optim") switches optimiser. With the default the general structure does not converge here. If a mixed model fails to converge, trying another optimiser is a reasonable first step — but if several fail, treat that as evidence the model is asking too much of the data rather than a technical nuisance.


3.2. diagonal covariance structure,













The next-least-restrictive option allows different variances but still no
covariance between the random intercept and slope — a diagonal G.



What this shows

pdDiag allows the intercept and slope to have different variances but still forces their covariance to zero. The two standard deviations printed are on quite different scales, because one is a weight and the other a weight per day.


3.3. general covariance structure.
Again, the option method in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method.













The general structure is the unrestricted one you already fitted. Compare all
three with `anova()`.



What this shows

The three G structures are nested, so the likelihood ratio tests in this table are meaningful.
If the diagonal structure is not clearly beaten by the general one, prefer it: the extra covariance parameter is buying little, and a simpler G is easier to interpret and more stable to fit.



Refit the selected model so far, but using the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation method this time.














Refit with `method = "REML"`. ML underestimates variance components because it
ignores the degrees of freedom used estimating the fixed effects; REML corrects
for that. Now that the structure is settled, REML gives better variance
estimates.
Try `run_app("lmm_simulator")` with a small number of subjects to watch this
happen.



What this shows

Refitting with REML now that the structure is settled. ML underestimates variance components because it does not pay for having estimated the fixed effects; REML corrects that. The fixed effects barely move — it is the variance components that change.
run_app("lmm_simulator") with a small number of subjects shows this directly.



Based on the selected model, fitted using the REML method, answer the following questions:
5.1. Produce the standardised residuals plot (i.e., residuals against fitted values) and the residual qqnorm plot. Justify whether the fitted model is good.














Two plots. The first is standardised residuals against fitted values — look for
constant spread. The second is a normal QQ plot of those residuals.
`plot(fit, resid(., type = "p") ~ fitted(.))` gives the first.



What this shows

Standardised residuals against fitted values. You are looking for a horizontal band of roughly constant width. A funnel shape would suggest the variance grows with the mean and a transformation is needed; curvature would suggest the mean model is wrong.


5.2. Justify whether the predicted random effects are normally distributed (for example check the qqnorm plot).













Random effects are not residuals, so the formula inside `qqnorm()` must extract
the predicted random effects rather than `resid(.)`. You are checking the
assumption b_i ~ N(0, G).



What this shows

This is a different assumption from the last plot. Here you are checking \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) — that the animals are normally distributed around the population, not that the residuals are. Points close to the line support it; a few stragglers are worth identifying, since they are individual animals behaving unusually rather than individual measurements.


5.3. Give the 95% confidence intervals for the estimates of fixed effects and variance components. Explain whether or not they are significant.













One `nlme` function returns confidence intervals for the fixed effects, the
variance components and the correlation parameters together. An interval for a variance
that nearly touches zero is telling you something.



What this shows

Confidence intervals for the fixed effects. The interaction is the one to read: if its interval excludes zero, the two groups genuinely differ in growth rate, which is the scientific question.
Interpret the interval, not just whether it contains zero. An interval from 0.01 to 0.9 excludes zero but is consistent with an effect too small to matter.


5.4. Plot the predicted mean lines of the two treatment groups in a single figure. Comment on the plot.













Predict from the fitted model at each day for each treatment group, then plot
the two curves together. The gap between them is the treatment effect.



What this shows

Population-level predictions, level = 0, meaning the average animal in each group rather than any particular animal.
The two curves cross, which is what the raw means suggested in week 1. Group A starts heavier and group B overtakes it — a difference in slope, which is exactly what the interaction term encodes.


5.5. Plot the estimated line and the real observations for the first two cattle in each group. Comment on the plots.













Subset to the four animals, use `predict()` for their fitted lines, then overlay
the observed points. Because these are subject-specific predictions, the lines
should track individual animals more closely than the group means did.



What this shows

Subject-specific predictions, the default level = 1, which add each animal’s own random intercept and slope.
Compare these with the group-level curves from the previous item: they track the individual points much more closely. That gap between the population line and the subject line is the random effect, and its size is what \(\mathbf{G}\) measures.

title: Week 3 tutorial: Inference for linear mixed models
section: Q2: how far a predicted random effect is pulled towards the mean
text:
Q2: how far a predicted random effect is pulled towards the mean
Q1 item 5.2 asked you to check the random-effects assumption with a QQ plot of the predicted \(\hat b_i\). This section asks what those predictions actually are. They are not the per-subject averages you would get by fitting each subject separately, and the difference has a formula.
The cd4 data are used because the number of observations per subject varies from 1 to 12, and the amount of shrinkage depends on exactly that.

Fit a random intercept model for \(\sqrt{\text{CD4}}\) on time, then verify the shrinkage formula: the predicted random effect equals the subject’s mean raw deviation multiplied by \(k_i = \sigma_b^2/(\sigma_b^2+\sigma^2/n_i)\).














The "raw deviation" must be measured from the population line, ignoring the
random effects: that is `residuals(fit, level = 0)`. Level 1 would already have
the random effect removed, which is the thing you are trying to reconstruct.
The shrinkage factor divides the residual variance by the number of observations
that subject contributed, `n_i`.
If you have it right, `blup` and `k * raw` agree to numerical precision.



What this shows

\(\hat\sigma_b^2 = 19.52\), \(\hat\sigma^2 = 19.89\), and the largest discrepancy between \(\hat b_i\) and \(k_i \bar e_i\) across all 369 men is about \(4 \times 10^{-8}\) — zero, up to the optimiser’s tolerance.
So the BLUP is not a new quantity at all. It is the subject’s own average departure from the population line, multiplied by a number between 0 and 1. All the content is in \(k_i\):
\[k_i = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2/n_i}.\]
Read the two extremes. As \(n_i \to \infty\), \(k_i \to 1\) and the subject is believed entirely. As \(n_i \to 0\) information, \(k_i \to 0\) and the subject is given the population mean. Everything in between is a weighted compromise, with the weight set by how much that particular subject has told you.



Plot the predicted random effects against the raw deviations, and tabulate the average shrinkage factor by how many observations a subject contributed. Who gets pulled the furthest?














`tapply()` needs a function to apply within each group of `n_i`: you want the
average shrinkage factor, so that function is `mean`.
The last line compares the spread of the raw deviations with the spread of the
predictions. Shrinkage is a statement about that spread, so the second argument
is `blup`.



What this shows

The scatter falls inside the 45 degree line everywhere, and the fan shape is the interesting part: points do not all lie on one line through the origin, because each has its own slope \(k_i\).
Average shrinkage factor by number of observations:



\(n_i\)
1
2
3-4
5-8
9-12




mean \(k_i\)
0.495
0.663
0.779
0.861
0.907



A man seen once has his apparent deviation halved — the model does not believe half of what a single observation says, because a single observation carries as much noise as signal when \(\sigma_b^2 \approx \sigma^2\). A man seen ten or more times keeps about 91% of his, because by then his own data outweigh the population.
The spread confirms it: the raw deviations have standard deviation 4.81, the predictions 4.05. The distribution of estimated subject effects is genuinely narrower than the distribution of the raw averages, which is what “shrinkage” names.
Two consequences worth carrying forward.
A ranking of subjects by BLUP is not a ranking by raw average. The poorly-observed subjects are pulled towards the middle, so they are unlikely to appear at either extreme. That is usually a feature — the extremes of a raw ranking are dominated by whoever had the fewest observations — but it means you cannot read a BLUP as “this subject’s level”.
This is the same mechanism as the CAR models in week 10. There, an area with few expected cases has its relative risk pulled towards its neighbours’ for exactly this reason: little information of its own, so the prior does more of the work. The formula is different, the idea is identical.

title: Week 3 tutorial: Inference for linear mixed models
text:
Week 3 complete




What you have learnt
You have taken a linear mixed model from specification to a checked, interpreted fit.

Writing the model in matrix form, and seeing why the random slope makes the marginal variance grow with time — animals fan out.
Model selection in two stages: settle \(\mathbf{R}_i\) first with \(\mathbf{G}\) held general, then settle \(\mathbf{G}\). Doing both at once searches a much larger space for no good reason.
ML versus REML. ML is required when comparing models with different fixed effects; REML gives less biased variance components once the structure is fixed. Refitting the chosen model with REML is the standard last step.
Diagnostics. Standardised residuals against fitted values for constant spread; a QQ plot of residuals; and separately a QQ plot of the predicted random effects, which checks \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) and is a different assumption from the residual one.
Inference and prediction. Confidence intervals for fixed effects and variance components together, and subject-specific predictions that track individual animals rather than the group mean.

Worth trying: run_app("lmm_simulator") with a small number of subjects — you can watch ML underestimate the between-subject standard deviation while REML does not.

title: Week 5 tutorial: Generalised estimating equations
text: Week 5 — Generalised estimating equations

title: Week 5 tutorial: Generalised estimating equations
text:
Overview
Weeks 2 to 4 modelled the correlation within a subject explicitly, through random effects and a structure for \(\mathbf{R}_i\). Generalised estimating equations take the opposite approach: specify only the mean, treat the correlation as a nuisance to be guessed at, and repair the standard errors afterwards. The result is consistent even when the guess is wrong — which is both the method’s strength and the source of most of the confusion about it.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

write down a marginal model for a binary longitudinal response;
fit it by GEE, choosing a working correlation structure;
explain the difference between the naive and the robust (sandwich) standard errors, and say which to report;
see for yourself that the estimates barely move when the working correlation changes, while the standard errors do; and
distinguish a marginal, population-averaged coefficient from a subject-specific one.


The data
The Indonesian Children’s Health Study (ichs) followed 250 preschool children, examined at an initial clinic visit and then every three months for fifteen months — at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 months, so 1500 observations in all. The question is whether children with vitamin A deficiency are at greater risk of respiratory infection.







Column
Description




id
child identifier


infection
respiratory infection: 0 = absent, 1 = present — the response


time
months since the first visit


gender
0 = male, 1 = female


vitA
vitamin A status: 0 = not deficient, 1 = deficient


age
age in years



The code below copies the data to ICHS and renames these columns to ID, Y, Time, Gender, VitaminA and age, so that the model formulae read closer to the notation used in the lectures. Both names refer to the same column.

title: Week 5 tutorial: Generalised estimating equations
section: Q1: fitting a marginal model by GEE
text:
Q1: fitting a marginal model by GEE

Let \(Y_i\) be the vector of responses for the \(i\)th child, consisting of the elements \(Y_{ij}\), which are observations on whether the child has a respiratory infection at time \(t_{ij}\) (recorded in months; Yes=1 and No=0). Write down a model for \(E(Y_{ij})\) with an appropriate link function, linear in an intercept and additive terms for time, age, gender and vitamin A status. Write down \(\mbox{Var}(Y_{ij})\) as well, given the nature of the response.
Fit the model from part (1) without accounting for the within-subject correlation — that is, treating all 1500 observations as independent.
Is there evidence that respiratory infection is associated with vitamin A deficiency? State the null hypothesis in terms of the parameters of your model, give the test statistic and p-value you base the answer on, and state your conclusion.











`geese()` (or `geeglm()`) from `geepack`. For "ignoring the correlation", the
working correlation is `corstr = "independence"`.
The response is binary, so `family = binomial`, and `id = ID` tells the function
which rows belong to the same child.
Look at the Wald test for the vitamin A coefficient.



What this shows

This is the independence working correlation — the deliberately naive fit that pretends the six visits per child are unrelated.
Read the vitamin A row. The estimate is about 0.29 on the log-odds scale, so \(\exp(0.29) \approx 1.33\): about a third higher odds of infection for a deficient child. But the Wald p-value is around 0.20, so on this evidence the association is not statistically significant.
Note that geese reports sandwich standard errors by default, in the san.se column. Even in this fit, the standard errors are already robust to the correlation being wrong.



Write down a model that extends the model in part (1) by taking into account the within-subject correlation among repeated measurements.
Fit the model from part (3). Assuming the working correlation is adequate, test the same null hypothesis as in part (2).
Does your conclusion agree with the one you reached in part (2)? Using the R output, explain why the two differ or agree, and justify which model you would report.














Refit with `corstr = "exchangeable"`, `"ar1"` and `"unstructured"` in turn.
The point of the exercise is what changes and what does not: compare the
estimates across the four fits, then compare their standard errors.
The estimates should barely move; the standard errors will.



What this shows

The whole point of the week is in this comparison, so read it carefully.
The estimates barely move across the four working correlations. Vitamin A goes from about 0.287 under independence to about 0.276 under exchangeable, a change far smaller than its standard error. That is the consistency result happening in front of you: get the working correlation wrong and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is still fine.
The robust standard errors barely move either — around 0.223 in both. That is not a coincidence: the sandwich estimator builds the covariance from the observed residuals rather than from the assumed structure, so it does not care much which structure you assumed. Had you looked at the naive standard errors instead, they would have moved a great deal.
The estimated exchangeable correlation is about 0.51, which is substantial: two visits on the same child are strongly related, and the independence assumption was clearly false. It simply did not damage the estimates.
run_app("gee_robustness") shows the other half of this: the naive standard error is wrong by tens of per cent while the robust one holds. Which way it is wrong depends on the covariate. For one that varies within a subject, as in the app, ignoring positive correlation makes the naive standard error too large; for one that varies between subjects, such as vitA here, it makes it too small — which is the dangerous direction, because it overstates the evidence.



Is there evidence that the probability of respiratory infection changes over the fifteen months of the study? And is there evidence that gender is worth keeping in the model?














Two separate questions. For time, look at the coefficient on `Time`. For gender,
compare a model with and without it — but note you cannot use a likelihood ratio
test here, because GEE is not likelihood-based. Use the Wald test, or QIC.



What this shows

Two separate questions, answered by dropping one term at a time.
For time, the coefficient is small and positive with a p-value near 0.04, so there is modest evidence that infection risk changes over the fifteen months.
For gender, the coefficient is around -0.56 with a p-value near 0.01, so it is worth keeping: girls have appreciably lower odds of infection than boys in this cohort.
A methodological note. You cannot compare these models with a likelihood ratio test, because GEE specifies only the first two moments and has no likelihood. Use the Wald tests shown, or QIC if you want a selection criterion.
Finally, remember what these coefficients mean. They are population-averaged log odds ratios, comparing groups of children. They are not the change for an individual child, which is what the GLMM in week 4 estimated. For a logit link the two differ, and reporting one as the other misdescribes the finding.

title: Week 5 tutorial: Generalised estimating equations
section: Q2: what the working correlation does, and does not, change
text:
Q2: what the working correlation does, and does not, change
Items 2 and 4 fitted the same mean model under four working correlations. This section makes the comparison explicit, and then asks which of the two competing answers about vitamin A you should report.

Build a table with one row per working correlation, holding the vitamin A coefficient, its naive standard error and its robust standard error. Which column moves between rows, and which does not?














`geese` keeps the naive (model-based) covariance matrix of the coefficients in
`fit$vbeta.naiv`; its diagonal holds the squared naive standard errors.
The robust ones are already in the summary's mean table, in the column called
`san.se` — "san" for sandwich.
Read down the estimate column first, then across to the two standard errors.



What this shows




working
estimate
naive SE
robust SE




independence
0.287
0.117
0.223


exchangeable
0.276
0.220
0.223


AR(1)
0.283
0.218
0.228



Read it column by column.
The estimate spans 0.276 to 0.287 — a four per cent spread across three quite different assumptions about the correlation. This is consistency under misspecification, happening in front of you. The working correlation is a working assumption.
The robust standard error is near 0.22 in every row. It does not care which working correlation you chose, which is exactly the property that makes it worth using.
The naive standard error is the one that moves, and it is the dangerous one. Under independence it is 0.117, barely half the robust value. A Wald test built on it would use a standard error about half what the data support, and the vitamin A effect would look roughly twice as significant as it is. Under exchangeable and AR(1) the naive and robust values nearly agree — because those working correlations are close to the truth for these data.
That is the rule in practice: report robust standard errors always, and treat close agreement between naive and robust as weak evidence that your working correlation was reasonable.



geeglm() reports QIC, the GEE analogue of AIC. Compute it for the three working correlations and say which you would choose — and how much the choice matters here.














`QIC()` is in `geepack`. Use `geeglm()` rather than `geese()` — the two fit the
same model, but only `geeglm` objects carry what `QIC()` needs.
The other two working correlations are `"exchangeable"` and `"ar1"`.
Look at the CIC column as well as QIC: CIC is the part that judges the
correlation model specifically.



What this shows

QIC comes out at 1811.92, 1811.93 and 1813.76 for independence, exchangeable and AR(1).
The first two are separated by 0.01, which is nothing — QIC differences below about 2 are not worth acting on. AR(1) is about two units worse. So the honest reading is that the data cannot distinguish independence from exchangeable here, and mildly prefer either to AR(1).
That may feel unsatisfying, and it is worth sitting with. QIC is a criterion for the whole fit; the CIC column (14.69, 14.68, 15.42) isolates the part that judges the correlation model, and it tells the same story.
Note what this does not mean. Independence scoring well does not mean the observations are independent — the estimated exchangeable correlation is \(\hat\alpha = 0.51\), which is substantial. It means that for estimating this mean model, assuming independence and repairing the standard errors with the sandwich costs you very little efficiency. That is a statement about efficiency, not about the biology.



In week 4 you fitted this same model as a GLMM and got about 0.60 for vitamin A by adaptive quadrature. Here you get about 0.28. Both are correct. Explain what each estimates, and say which you would report to a health ministry deciding whether to fund a vitamin A programme.

title: Week 5 tutorial: Generalised estimating equations
text:
Week 5 complete




What you have learnt
You have fitted generalised estimating equations to binary longitudinal data.

The marginal model. GEE specifies only the mean and the variance, not the full distribution. For binary data the mean is on the logit scale and \(\text{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \phi\,\mu_{ij}(1-\mu_{ij})\).
The working correlation matrix. Independence, exchangeable, AR(1) or unstructured — a working assumption, not a claim you have to defend.
The central result. \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) stays consistent even when the working correlation is wrong, provided the mean model is right. The naive standard errors do not; the robust sandwich estimator repairs them.
Comparing fits. You saw the estimates barely move across working correlations while the standard errors moved a lot. That is the theory happening in front of you.
Marginal versus subject-specific. A GEE coefficient is a population-averaged log odds ratio. A GLMM coefficient is subject-specific. They are not equal for a logit link, and reporting the wrong one misdescribes the finding.
No likelihood. GEE is not likelihood-based, so no likelihood ratio tests. Use Wald tests or QIC.

Worth trying: run_app("gee_robustness") — set the truth to exchangeable and the working correlation to independence, and watch the slope stay unbiased while the naive standard error goes badly wrong.

title: Week 8 tutorial: Geostatistical modelling and prediction
text: Week 8 — Kriging and spatial prediction

title: Week 8 tutorial: Geostatistical modelling and prediction
text:
Overview
Last week you established that the Galicia residuals are spatially correlated. This week you put that correlation into a model and use it to predict.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

fit a linear geostatistical model, with and without a nugget, and say what the difference buys you;
interpret the estimated covariance parameters;
predict at unobserved locations, with and without a covariate; and
compute and map summaries of the predictive distribution, including exceedance probabilities.


The data
The same galicia data as last week: lead concentration measured in moss at 132 sampling stations across Galicia, in north-west Spain, with a co-located measurement of airborne particulate matter.



Column
Description




lead
lead concentration


loglead
log lead concentration — the response


long
longitude, decimal degrees


lat
latitude, decimal degrees


pm10
particulate matter under 10 micrometres



Two further objects are used for prediction: galicia_grid, a 1 km grid covering the region, and galicia_pred, which holds PM10 at each grid point so that a model with the covariate can be used to predict.
As last week, RiskMap ships a different dataset also called galicia, so load this one with data(galicia, package = "lsda").

title: Week 8 tutorial: Geostatistical modelling and prediction
section: Q1: fitting a linear geostatistical model
text:
Q1: fitting a linear geostatistical model

Fit three linear geostatistical models to the log-transformed lead concentration. In each, \(S(x_i)\) is a stationary Gaussian process with a Matérn correlation function and \(\kappa = 1.5\).

Model 1 — no covariate and no nugget: \[\begin{equation}\label{eq:glgm_no_cov}
   \log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + S(x_i),
\end{equation}\]
Model 2 — no covariate, but with a nugget: \[\begin{equation}\label{eq:glgm_no_cov_nug}
   \log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + S(x_i) + Z_i,
\end{equation}\] where the \(Z_i\) are independent Gaussian variables with variance \(\tau^2\). What does the estimated nugget tell you about how much it matters here?
Model 3 — PM10 as a covariate, no nugget: \[\begin{equation}\label{eq:glgm_lin}
   \log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 d(x_i) + S(x_i),
\end{equation}\] where \(d(x_i)\) is PM10 at location \(x_i\). How does adding \(d(x_i)\) change the estimated covariance parameters?












Three calls to `glgpm()`. The formula controls all three differences:
`loglead ~ gp(kappa = 1.5)` for the first, add `nugget = NULL` inside `gp()` to
estimate a nugget, and put `pm10 +` before `gp()` to add the covariate.
Watch what happens to the nugget estimate and to its confidence interval.



What this shows

Three fits, differing only in the formula.
Model 2 versus model 1. The nugget is estimated at about 0.00087, roughly 2.7% of the spatial variance, with a confidence interval running to infinity — completely uninformative. The log-likelihood is identical to model 1 to four decimal places, so the extra parameter has bought no fit at all.
This is a design consequence, not a failure. The nugget describes behaviour at distances shorter than the closest pair of stations, and the Galicia network has very few such pairs, so the likelihood is almost flat in \(\tau^2\). If you need to estimate a nugget, put close pairs into the design deliberately.
Model 3. PM10 enters with a coefficient around 0.011 and a Wald p-value below 0.001. Note also what happened to the covariance parameters: the process variance falls from 0.0323 to 0.0304 and the correlation scale from 9.02 to 7.86 km. The covariate has absorbed part of the spatial structure, because PM10 is itself spatially smooth. Fixed and random parts of a spatial model are not separable.
One caution before you conclude PM10 matters. The likelihood ratio test gives \(2 \times (180.80 - 179.12) = 3.35\) on 1 degree of freedom, so \(p \approx 0.067\) — much weaker than the Wald test suggests. The Wald test holds the covariance parameters fixed at their estimates while the likelihood ratio test lets them re-estimate, and here they move noticeably. When the two disagree, trust the likelihood ratio test.



Which of the three models do you consider the best? Justify your choice.
Interpret the estimated parameters of the model you chose. Say what each one means in the units of the problem, not just whether it is significant.














`coef()` gives the estimated parameters. The two to interpret are the spatial
process variance and the correlation scale phi.
Phi is not itself the distance at which correlation dies away — convert it to a
practical range, the distance at which correlation falls to about 0.05. For a
Matern with kappa = 1.5 that is roughly 4.7 times phi; solve it properly with
`uniroot()`.



What this shows

\(\phi\) is a scale parameter, not a distance at which correlation dies away — the multiplier depends on the smoothness \(\kappa\). Converting it gives a practical range of about 43 km for model 1 and 37 km for model 3: the distance beyond which correlation has fallen to roughly 0.05.
Report the practical range, not \(\phi\). It is the number a collaborator can interpret, and it is what tells you how far the data can reach when predicting.



Using Model 1 and Model 3, predict log lead concentration across Galicia on a 1 km grid, using galicia_grid for the locations and galicia_pred for PM10 at those locations. Map both the predicted values and their standard errors.














Prediction needs a grid (`galicia_grid`) and, for the model with the covariate,
the covariate at each grid point (`galicia_pred`).
Map both the predicted mean and the standard error. The second map is the one
that tells you where to trust the first.



What this shows

Two maps, and the second is as important as the first.
The prediction surface is smooth and looks equally confident everywhere, which it is not.
The standard error surface shows why. Uncertainty is low around the stations and rises in the gaps and towards the edges, where prediction becomes extrapolation. The kriging variance is \(\sigma^2 - \mathbf{c}_0^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{c}_0\): near data the subtracted term is large, and far away the correlations decay to nothing and the variance returns to the prior variance, meaning the model has nothing to add beyond the overall mean.
The scale over which that happens is the practical range from item 3 — about 43 km. A location further than that from any station is effectively uninformed.
Presenting the prediction map without the uncertainty map invites exactly the over-confident reading the model was fitted to avoid. If the question is whether lead exceeds a threshold, give an exceedance probability, which uses both.



Compare the two sets of predictions. Where do they agree, where do they differ, and which is more certain?
Where is the predictive uncertainty lowest? Explain why, in terms of the estimated spatial structure and where the sampling stations are.

title: Week 8 tutorial: Geostatistical modelling and prediction
text:
Challenge
Build a binomial geostatistical model for onchocerciasis (river blindness) prevalence in Liberia, and investigate its relationship with log elevation.
The response is now a count out of a total rather than a continuous measurement, so this extends everything above to the generalised case.
Load the data with data("liberia", package = "RiskMap") — name the package, because the course package carries a different dataset under the same name. It holds nodule counts from 90 sampled villages:



Column
Description




lat, long
latitude and longitude of the village


ntest
number of people tested for the presence of nodules


npos
number testing positive


elevation
village elevation, metres


log_elevation
log of elevation















What this shows

glgpm() fits the binomial model by Monte Carlo maximum likelihood, and the Monte Carlo error can be large relative to the reported standard errors. On these data, refitting with different seeds gave log-elevation estimates from 0.23 to 0.41, each with a reported standard error of about 0.02. Before trusting a fit, refit it with another seed, and with more samples through control_mcmc = set_control_sim(n_sim = ...), and check the estimates agree.
For reference, the maximum likelihood fit (computed with the Laplace approximation and checked by profiling the likelihood over the range) gives 0.337 (SE 0.068) for log elevation, a spatial variance of 0.087 and a range of about 46 km. Doubling elevation multiplies the odds of nodules by \(e^{0.337 \ln 2} = 1.26\) (95% CI 1.15 to 1.39). The standard error is larger than the binomial GLM’s (0.040) because the model now allows for spatial correlation.

title: Week 8 tutorial: Geostatistical modelling and prediction
section: Q2: the lecture example, and the question a map is usually asked
text:
Q2: the lecture example, and the question a map is usually asked
The Galicia analysis above predicts a surface. A surface is rarely the decision; the decision is usually whether somewhere is over a limit. This section repeats the modelling on the data from the lectures and then produces the summary that answers that question directly.
gm_no2 holds nitrogen dioxide at 25 monitoring stations across Greater Manchester, with distance to the nearest major road as a covariate, and gm_grid is a 4996-point grid covering the conurbation carrying the same covariate.

Fit the model from the lectures — NO\(_2\) on road distance with a Matérn spatial process — and predict over gm_grid. Map the predictive mean and the predictive standard error.














The covariate is `road`, the distance to the nearest major road in metres.
`pred_over_grid()` needs two things that must agree: the locations to predict at,
`st_geometry(gm_grid)`, and a data frame holding the covariates at those same
locations — which is `gm_grid` itself.
`fix_var_me = 0` says there is no measurement error, so the nugget in `gp()` is
the only non-spatial term.



What this shows

The road coefficient is about \(-0.0079\) per metre. Multiply by 1000: every kilometre further from a major road takes about 7.9 units off the predicted NO\(_2\). The spatial process variance is about 105 with a correlation scale of 14.7 km, so there is substantial structure left over and above the road effect.
The predictive mean runs from about 18 to 72 across the grid, and the standard error from 0.26 to 5.3. Compare the two maps: the standard error is smallest near the 25 stations and grows with distance from them, which is the same behaviour you saw for Galicia. A surface that looks equally smooth everywhere is not equally trustworthy everywhere.
Twenty-five stations is a small design for a region this size. That is realistic — monitoring networks are expensive — and it is why the uncertainty map matters more here, not less.



The UK annual mean limit value for NO\(_2\) is 40 µg/m\(^3\). Recompute the prediction summaries to include the probability that each grid cell exceeds it, and map that. How many cells is the model confident about, and how many is it genuinely unsure about?














`pred_over_grid()` has already drawn samples from the predictive distribution at
every grid cell; `pd_summary` just says how to summarise them. The proportion of
samples above 40 is the estimated probability of exceeding 40 — and the
proportion of a logical vector is its `mean`.
Nothing needs refitting: the same `no2.pred` object is being summarised a second
way.



What this shows

Of the 4996 cells, about 4192 have \(P(\text{NO}_2 > 40) > 0.9\), about 414 have it below 0.1, and roughly 390 sit in between.
That last number is the useful one. Those 390 cells are where the data cannot say which side of the limit the truth falls, and they are a different set from “the cells near 40 on the mean map”. A cell whose predictive mean is 45 with a standard error of 5 is genuinely uncertain; a cell whose mean is 45 with a standard error of 0.3 is not. Thresholding the mean map at 40 throws that distinction away, and it is the distinction a regulator needs — it tells you where another monitor would change a decision.
Note what the exceedance map is not: it is not a map of where NO\(_2\) is high. It combines level and uncertainty. A cell can have a low predicted level and a middling exceedance probability if the prediction there is poor, and that is the intended behaviour.
One caution. These probabilities are computed with the covariance parameters held at their estimates. They are plug-in probabilities, so they are slightly over-confident for the same reason plug-in prediction intervals are too narrow.



Not every dataset has spatial structure worth modelling. Fit a Gaussian geostatistical model to the liberia data in the course package — height-for-age z-scores for 267 clusters, with the local malaria incidence rate as a covariate — and decide from the output whether the spatial term is earning its place.














The covariate is `malaria_incidence_rate`.
Then compare two numbers in the output: the spatial process variance and the
measurement error variance. Which of the two is doing the work?
`propose_utm()` picks a sensible projected CRS, because a Matérn
correlation needs distances, and degrees are not distances.



What this shows

Malaria incidence enters at about \(-1.18\) with a standard error of 0.15, so \(p < 10^{-15}\): clusters with higher malaria incidence have markedly lower height-for-age. One unit of incidence costs more than a whole z-score.
Now the covariance parameters, which are the point of the exercise. The spatial process variance is about 0.015 against a measurement error variance of about 0.400 — the spatial term accounts for under 4% of the residual variation. The confidence interval for the spatial variance runs from 0.004 to 0.062, close to the boundary.
So the honest conclusion is that once malaria incidence is in the model there is very little spatial structure left. Compare Galicia, where the spatial variance was the dominant term and dropping it would have been wrong.
This is worth meeting deliberately, because a geostatistical model will always fit. Whether the spatial part is doing anything is a question you have to ask of the output, and the answer is sometimes no. When it is no, say so: a simple regression with independent errors is easier to explain and easier to defend, and the covariate has done the work.

title: Week 8 tutorial: Geostatistical modelling and prediction
text:
Week 8 complete




What you have learnt
You have fitted geostatistical models and used them to predict.

The linear geostatistical model. \(\log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + S(x_i) + Z_i\), with \(S\) a stationary Gaussian process and \(Z_i\) a nugget.
The nugget is not free. Its estimate was essentially zero with an infinite upper confidence limit, because the design has almost no close pairs. A parameter you cannot identify is a parameter you should not fit — and if you want to estimate a nugget, put close pairs in the design deliberately.
Covariates change the covariance. Adding PM10 reduced both the process variance and the correlation scale: the covariate absorbed part of the spatial structure. Fixed and random parts of a spatial model are not independent of each other.
Wald and likelihood ratio tests can disagree. They did here for PM10. The Wald test holds the covariance parameters fixed; the likelihood ratio test lets them re-estimate, which is why it is the safer guide.
Phi is not the range. Convert it to a practical range — the distance at which correlation has decayed to about 0.05 — before interpreting it.
Kriging, and its uncertainty. Prediction variance is smallest near the data and rises towards the process variance as you move away. The map of standard errors is as important as the map of predictions; showing one without the other invites over-confidence.

Overview
Last week you found spatial autocorrelation in the Scottish lip cancer data and saw that raw SIRs are unstable in counties with few expected cases. This week you fit models that address both: the spatial correlation is built into the model, and estimates for small counties borrow strength from their neighbours.
By the end of this sheet you should be able to:

fit a Poisson model for areal counts with spatially structured random effects;
map the estimated relative risk together with its uncertainty;
compute posterior probabilities such as \(\Pr(\theta_i > 2)\); and
compare CAR specifications and choose between them.

title: Week 10 tutorial: Area-level modelling with CAR models
section: Q1: fitting a CAR model to areal counts
text:
Q1: fitting a CAR model to areal counts

Fit a model assuming that the observed cancer cases, \(Y_i\), are conditionally independently Poisson distributed:

\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i \theta_i), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n,
\]
where \(E_i\) is the expected cancer cases and \(\theta_i\) is the relative risk in county \(i\). The logarithm of \(\theta_i\) is expressed as:
\[
\log(\theta_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{aff}_i + \phi_i,
\]
where:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept representing the overall risk,
\(\beta_1\) is the coefficient of the covariate \(\text{aff}_i\),
\(\phi_i\) is a random effect with the Leroux conditional autoregressive (CAR) prior: \[
  \phi_i \mid \phi_{-i} \sim N\left(\frac{\rho\sum_j w_{ij}\phi_j}{\rho\sum_j w_{ij} + 1 - \rho}, \frac{\tau^2}{\rho\sum_j w_{ij} + 1 - \rho}\right),
  \] where \(\rho \in [0,1]\) is estimated: \(\rho = 0\) gives independent random effects and \(\rho = 1\) the intrinsic CAR model. Like the BYM model, which adds a structured and an unstructured random effect, this lets the data decide the balance between spatially structured and unstructured variation, but with a single set of random effects.











Two steps. First build the adjacency matrix from shared borders, as in week 9.
Three island groups have no neighbours, and CARBayes requires every area to have
at least one, so each island is joined to its nearest county (the code does this
for you). Then `S.CARleroux()` with `family = "poisson"`, the AFF covariate, and
`offset(log(expected))`; leave `rho` unset so that it is estimated.
The offset is what turns a count model into a relative risk model: without it
you would be modelling raw counts rather than counts relative to what is
expected.



What this shows

Two things are happening here.
The adjacency matrix is built from shared borders, as in week 9. Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles share no border with any county, and CARBayes needs every row of \(W\) to have a positive sum, so each is joined to its nearest county. Do not solve this with a large snap tolerance: the geometry is in metres, and snap = 200000 makes almost every county a neighbour of every other (about 47 of the other 55), which wipes out the spatial structure: Moran’s \(I\) of the SIR falls from 0.44 to 0.05.
Then S.CARleroux fits the Bayesian model by MCMC, with \(\rho\) estimated. Read the output for the aff coefficient and its credible interval (about 4.1, with a 95% interval of roughly 1.5 to 6.5), and for \(\rho\) (about 0.85: strong spatial dependence). Check the model has converged, for example with the Geweke diagnostics, before trusting anything else.
The offset(log(expected)) is doing essential work. Without it you are modelling the number of cases, which mostly reflects population size. With it, the linear predictor describes the log relative risk — how the observed count compares with what the county’s demographic structure predicts. That is the epidemiological quantity.



Map the estimated relative risk of lip cancer for each county, together with its uncertainty, and interpret what you see. Recall that the relative risk says whether county \(i\) is at higher (\(\theta_i > 1\)) or lower (\(\theta_i < 1\)) risk than the standard population.














Relative risk is the fitted value divided by the expected count.
`model$samples$fitted` holds the posterior samples, so the posterior mean gives
the estimate and the posterior standard deviation gives the uncertainty.
Map both, and compare the smoothed map with the raw SIR from week 9. The
smoothing is the model borrowing strength from neighbours — strongest where the
expected counts are small and the raw SIR is therefore noisiest.



What this shows

The smoothed relative risk, and its uncertainty, mapped.
Compare the smoothed map with the raw SIR map from week 9. The counties that move most are those with small expected counts: where the data are weak, the CAR prior pulls the estimate towards the neighbourhood average; where the data are strong, the likelihood dominates and the estimate barely moves.
That is borrowing strength, and it is the same idea as BLUP shrinkage in week 3 — a compromise between what one unit’s own data say and what its neighbours say, weighted by how much information the unit provides.
The uncertainty map matters as much as the estimate map. A relative risk of 1.9 means something quite different with a narrow posterior than with a wide one.

title: Week 10 tutorial: Area-level modelling with CAR models
text:
Challenge

Map the probability that the relative risk is greater than 2.














You have posterior samples of the relative risk, so the probability that it
exceeds 2 is just the proportion of samples above 2, computed area by area.
This is the kind of statement a public health decision actually needs: not a
point estimate, but how confident we are that risk is elevated.



What this shows

The posterior probability that relative risk exceeds 2, computed by counting the proportion of posterior samples above 2 for each county.
This is a more useful statement than a point estimate for anyone making a decision. “The estimated risk is 1.9” leaves open how confident we are; “\(P(\theta_i > 2 \mid \text{data}) = 0.8\)” answers the question directly. Being able to compute any functional of the posterior straight from the samples is one of the practical advantages of the Bayesian approach.



Fit another model where \(\phi_i\) is modelled using an intrinsic conditional autoregressive (ICAR) distribution














Same call, but the ICAR model is the limiting case with `rho` fixed at 1 — see
`S.CARleroux`'s arguments. Compare the fitted risks: ICAR assumes the spatial
structure is entirely local, so it tends to smooth more.



What this shows

The ICAR model fixes the spatial dependence parameter at its maximum, so all the area-level variation is assumed spatially structured.
Compare its fitted risks with the Leroux model’s. ICAR generally smooths more, because it has no way to represent an area effect that is simply idiosyncratic. Leroux estimates the balance between structured and unstructured variation instead of assuming it, which is usually the safer default — but it is worth seeing what the stronger assumption does to the map.

section: Q2: the lecture example, and choosing between CAR models
text:
Q2: the lecture example, and choosing between CAR models
The Scotland analysis used a Poisson likelihood with an offset, because the data were counts of cases against expected counts. The lecture example is a binomial one: of the children measured in each district, how many were obese. This section fits it, then asks how you would choose between the three random-effects structures the lectures introduced.
nw_obesity holds the 33 local authority districts of North West England, with num_obese out of total_sampled children and the district’s average IDACI score, a measure of income deprivation affecting children.

Build the adjacency matrix and fit the binomial ICAR model from the lectures. Does deprivation predict childhood obesity?














`poly2nb()` builds the neighbour list from shared borders. Set the row names on
the data first: given an `sf` object, `poly2nb()` takes its names from
`row.names(x)` and ignores a `row.names =` argument you pass it.
For a binomial model `trials` is the denominator — the number of children
measured, `total_sampled`.
Fixing `rho = 1` in `S.CARleroux` gives the intrinsic CAR model.



What this shows

Thirty-three districts, 4.42 neighbours on average, and no isolated areas — a contrast with Scotland, where Orkney, Shetland and the Western Isles had to be dealt with before anything else could happen. Not every geography has that problem, but you have to check rather than assume.
The IDACI coefficient is about 2.46 with a 95% credible interval of roughly (2.13, 2.80). The interval excludes zero comfortably, so there is strong evidence that deprivation is associated with higher childhood obesity.
Read the size of it on a scale you can interpret. IDACI runs from 0.058 to 0.307 across these districts, a spread of about 0.25. Multiplying by 2.46 gives about 0.62 on the log-odds scale between the least and most deprived district, an odds ratio of about 1.9 — obesity odds roughly doubling across the range of deprivation in the region. That is a large effect, and it is what the raw map already hinted at: Manchester, Knowsley and Liverpool sit at the top of both.



The lectures introduced three ways to structure the random effects: ICAR, BYM and Leroux. Fit all three to these data and compare them by DIC. Which would you report, and how much does the choice matter?














The Leroux model is `S.CARleroux` again, but this time **without** `rho = 1` — so
that $\rho$ is estimated rather than fixed. That is why it is not in `fit_args`.
`S.CARbym()` fits the convolution model, with a spatial and an unstructured
random effect side by side.
Compare three things across the rows: DIC, the effective number of parameters
`p.d`, and the width of the credible interval for IDACI.

Two things are worth taking from this table, and they point in opposite directions.
The covariate estimate is untouched. 2.465, 2.464, 2.463 — the three structures agree to three decimal places. If the IDACI effect is what you are reporting, the choice between them is very nearly irrelevant, and it would be wrong to present the comparison as though the conclusion hung on it.
The cost of flexibility is visible. The effective number of parameters climbs from 22.6 to 26.8, DIC gets worse by about 4.6, and the credible interval widens from 0.67 to 0.85 units. BYM has a spatial and an unstructured random effect for only 33 areas, and the data cannot identify both; you pay for that in precision. Leroux’s \(\hat\rho\) comes out at about 0.69 — some way below 1, but with 33 areas the DIC still prefers simply fixing it there.
So: report ICAR here, and say why. The general advice from the lectures — prefer Leroux, because it estimates the balance rather than assuming it — is sound when you have enough areas to estimate \(\rho\) well. With 33 it is a close call, and this is the honest version of model choice: not one criterion pronouncing a winner, but a check that the answer you care about survives the choice. It does.
A caveat on DIC. These are MCMC fits, so the numbers move a little from seed to seed. A gap of 4.6 is small. Refit with another seed before leaning on it.

title: Week 10 tutorial: Area-level modelling with CAR models
text:
Week 10 complete




What you have learnt
You have fitted Bayesian spatial models to area-level counts.

The hierarchy. Counts are Poisson given a relative risk; the log relative risk is a covariate effect plus a spatially structured random effect plus an unstructured one.
The offset does the work. offset(log(expected)) is what turns a model for counts into a model for relative risk. Without it you are modelling how many cases occur, not whether that is more than expected.
CAR models borrow strength. The conditional autoregressive prior says an area’s risk is like its neighbours’. The result is a smoothed map — and the smoothing is strongest exactly where the raw SIR was least reliable, in areas with small expected counts.
Structured and unstructured effects. The first is spatially correlated, the second is area-specific noise. The Leroux parameterisation lets the data decide the balance; ICAR fixes it at purely spatial.
Posterior samples answer real questions. From the samples you can compute the probability that relative risk exceeds 2 area by area. That is a far more useful statement for a public health decision than a point estimate.
MCMC needs checking. Burn-in, thinning and convergence are not formalities.
